title: Definition
body_md:
A non-singular Calabi-Yau threefold $\tilde X$ is 
{\it primitive} if there is no birational contraction $\tilde
X\rightarrow X$ with $X$ smoothable to a Calabi-Yau threefold which is not
deformation equivalent to $\tilde X$.
head: environment

title: Question
body_md:
Given a Calabi-Yau threefold $X$ with canonical
singularities, is $\operatorname{Def}(X)$ non-singular? If not, can we get some
reasonable dimension estimates for components of $\operatorname{Def}(X)$?
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\tilde X$ be a non-singular Calabi-Yau threefold,
and $\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow X$ be a birational contraction morphism,
such that $X$ has isolated complete intersection singularities. Then
there is a deformation of $X$ which smooths all singular points of $X$
except possibly the ordinary double points of $X$.

name: Theorem \ref{3.8}

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\tilde X$ be a non-singular Calabi-Yau threefold and
$\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow X$ a birational contraction such that $X$ is 
$\mathbb{Q}$-factorial and for each $P\in Sing(X)$, the germ $(X,P)$ is good.
Then $X$ is smoothable.

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow X$ be a primitive contraction
contracting a divisor $E$ to a point. Then $X$ is smoothable unless $E\cong\mathbb{P}^2$
or $F_1$.

body_md:
\label{(1.1)}
The general context from \cite{[41]} is as follows. Let $k$
be a field and let $\Lambda$ be
a complete Noetherian local $k$-algebra with residue field $k$ and maximal ideal
${\bf m}_{\Lambda}$. We denote by
${\bf C}_{\Lambda}$ the category of Artin local $\Lambda$-algebras with residue field
$k$ with local homomorphisms. We are interested in deformation
functors $D:{\bf C}_{\Lambda}\rightarrow {\bf Ens}$ (here ${\bf Ens}$ is the category
of sets), with $D(k)$ consisting of one element.
head: environment

body_md:
\label{(1.2)}
We will only consider functors $D$ which are pro-representable
or have a hull (miniversal space). Thus there is a complete
local
$\Lambda$-algebra $S$ with residue field $k$ and a morphism of functors
$\operatorname{Hom}(S,\cdot)\rightarrow D$. This morphism is an isomorphism if $D$ is
pro-represented by $S$. If $S$ is a hull of $D$, this morphism is only smooth and
induces an isomorphism on tangent spaces. Here
$\operatorname{Hom}$ denotes local
$\Lambda$-algebra homomorphisms.
We will always write $S\cong R/J$, where $R=\Lambda[[x_1,\ldots,x_r]]$
with maximal ideal ${\bf m}_{R}={\bf m}_{\Lambda}R+
(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$, and $J\subseteq {\bf m}_{\Lambda}R+
{\bf m}_R^2$  an ideal.
head: environment

body_md:
\label{(1.3)}
Following \cite{[18]}, set
\begin{align*}
A_n={} & k[t]/(t^{n+1})\\
B_n={} & A_n\otimes_k A_1=k[x,y]/(x^{n+1},y^2)\\
C_n= {} & B_{n-1}\times_{A_{n-1}} A_n=k[x,y]/(x^{n+1},x^ny,y^2)
\end{align*}
and let $\alpha_n:A_{n+1}\rightarrow A_n$, $\beta_n:B_n\rightarrow A_n$,
$\gamma_n:B_n\rightarrow C_n$, and $\xi_n:B_n\rightarrow B_{n-1}$ be the natural
maps. Define
$\epsilon_n:A_{n+1}\rightarrow B_n$ by $t\mapsto x+y$ and $\epsilon_n':A_n\rightarrow
C_n$ by $t\mapsto x+y$ also.
head: environment

body_md:
\label{(1.4)}
Now consider the case that $\Lambda=k$ and that $D$ is prorepresentable. For
$X_n\in D(A_n)$ we define the first order tangent space  of $X_n$, 
$$T^1(X_n/A_n)=\{Y_n\in D(B_n)\,|\,D(\beta_n)(Y_n)=X_n\}.$$
This set has a natural $A_n$-module structure
as follows. First, if
$\alpha,\beta\in T^1(X_n/A_n)$, we need to define $\alpha+\beta$. We have
$\alpha\times \beta\in D(B_n)\times_{D(A_n)} D(B_n)=D(B_n\times_{A_n} B_n)$ by
pro-representability. We have an isomorphism of $k$-algebras
\[
B_n\times_{A_n} B_n\cong
k[x,y,y']/(x^{n+1},y^2,yy',y'^2),
\] 
and there is a natural map 
$B_n\times_{A_n} B_n\rightarrow B_n$ via $x\mapsto x, y\mapsto y, y'\mapsto y$. 
Then
$\alpha+\beta$ is the image of $\alpha\times\beta$ in $D(B_n)$ under this map.
It is easy to check that $\alpha+\beta\in T^1(X_n/A_n)$. 

Secondly, if $a\in A_n$, we have the endomorphism $a:B_n\rightarrow B_n$ given
by $x\mapsto x$, $y\mapsto ay$. Then if $\alpha\in T^1(X_n/A_n)$, so is
$a\alpha=D(a)(\alpha)$.
head: environment

body_md:
\label{(1.5)} 
In this paper, we will on occasion work with functors which are not necessarily
pro-representable, but which do have a hull. The deformation functor $D$ has
a hull if and only if Schlessinger's conditions $(H_1)$-$(H_3)$ of 
\cite[Thm.~2.11]{[41]}
are satisfied. We recall these here. For any morphisms $A'\rightarrow A$,
$A''\rightarrow A$ in ${\bf C}_{\Lambda}$, there is a natural functorial map
$$\psi_{A',A'',A}:D(A'\times_A A'')\rightarrow D(A')\times_{D(A)} D(A'').$$
A surjective map $A'\rightarrow A$ in ${\bf C}_{\Lambda}$ is a {\it small extension}
if its kernel is a non-zero principal ideal $(t)$ such that ${\bf m}_{A'}(t)=0$.
 The conditions $(H_1)$-$(H_3)$ are:
\begin{itemize}
\item[$(H_1)$] $\psi_{A',A'',A}$ is a surjection whenever $A''\rightarrow A$ is a
small extension.
\item[$(H_2)$] $\psi_{A',A'',A}$ is a bijection when $A=k$, $A''=A_1$. 
\item[$(H_3)$] $\dim_k(T^1(X/k))<\infty$.
\end{itemize}

$(H_2)$ guarantees that $T^1(X/k)$ has a $k$-vector space structure as in \ref{(1.4)}.
If in addition
$$\hbox{$(H_4)$ $\psi_{A',A',A}$ is a bijection for any small extension
$A'\rightarrow A$\hfill}$$
is satisfied then $D$ is pro-representable. (This is also a part of 
\cite[Thm.~2.11]{[41]}).

label: eq:pushfoward property
body_md:
As pointed out in \cite{KawaErr}, the definition for $T^1(X_n/A_n)$
given in \ref{(1.4)} is not correct if $D$ is not pro-representable,
and in particular need not be a vector space.\footnote{The original version
of this paper tried to get around this issue by introducing a property
$(H_5)$. However, in (1.6) of the published version of this paper,
the functor $D_X$ does not satisfy condition $(H_5)$. The construction
given is not well-defined since the result depends on choices.
Indeed, if $X_{A'}$, $X_{A''}$, $X_A$ are deformations
of $X$, $X_{A'}\otimes_{A'} A\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\phi_1}} X_A\smash{
  \mathop{\longleftarrow}\limits^{\phi_2}} X_{A''}
\otimes_{A''} A$, with $\phi_1$, $\phi_2$ isomorphisms, then
the isomorphism class of
$(X,\mathcal{O}_{X_{A'}}\times_{\mathcal{O}_{X_A}} \mathcal{O}_{X_{A''}})$ will depend on the particular choice
of the isomorphisms $\phi_1$, $\phi_2$,
as an automorphism of $X_A$ may not lift
to an automorphism of $X_{A'}$ or $X_{A''}$.}
Instead, following \cite{KawaErr}, one may still define an appropriate
space if $D$ is defined as the functor of flat deformations of a ringed
space $(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$ defined over $\operatorname{Spec} k$. However, in this revision
we will take a more general view-point and instead use the language
of categories cofibred in groupoids as developed in \cite{Rim} and
exposited in \cite[Tag~06G7]{Stacks}. We refer the reader to 
the latter reference for the principle definitions. 

A category cofibred in groupoids is a category $\mathcal{D}$ equipped with a functor
$p:\mathcal{D}\rightarrow \mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}$ such that $p^{\mathrm{opp}}:
\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{opp}}\rightarrow \mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}^{\mathrm{opp}}$ 
is a category fibred
in groupoids. We write $\mathcal{D}(A)$ for the sub-category of
$\mathcal{D}$ over $A\in \mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}$; this is a groupoid. Further,
the definition of category fibred in groupoids tells us that
for a morphism $f:A\rightarrow B$ in $\mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}$, there is for
each $X$ an object in $\mathcal{D}(A)$ a push-forward object $f_*X$ in 
$\mathcal{D}(B)$ equipped with a morphism $X\rightarrow f_*X$ over $f$.
This push-forward object is unique up to unique isomorphism 
(see \cite[Tag 06SH]{Stacks}). Further, push-forward has the property
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:pushfoward property}
\substack{\hbox{Given $f:A\rightarrow B$, $g:B\rightarrow C$, there is
a unique morphism $f_*X \rightarrow (g\circ f)_*X$,}\\
\hbox{ and hence a unique
isomorphism $g_*f_*X \rightarrow (g\circ f)_* X$.}}
\end{equation}
This again follows
from the properties of categories cofibred in groupoids, see 
\cite[Tag 06GJ]{Stacks}.

We use the
convention that we write $D(A)$ for the set of isomorphism classes
of $\mathcal{D}(A)$. This gives a functor $D:\mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}\rightarrow
\mathbf{Ens}$ given by $A\mapsto D(A)$.

\begin{example}
\label{ex:principal}
The principal example for us is given by deformations of a ringed space
$(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$ defined over $\operatorname{Spec} k$. Objects are data $(X_A,\mathcal{O}_{X_A})$
flat over $\operatorname{Spec} A$ and an isomorphism $\phi_{X_A}:X_A\otimes_A k\cong
X$. (Here we write $(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y) \otimes_A B$ for $(Y,\mathcal{O}_Y\otimes_A B)$.)
A morphism $X_A\rightarrow X_B$ lying over a homomorphism $A\rightarrow B$
is an isomorphism $X_A\otimes_A B \cong X_B$ compatible with the
isomorphisms $\phi_{X_A},\phi_{X_B}$. This is an example of a predeformation
category, see \cite[Tag 06GS]{Stacks}, in that $\mathcal{D}(k)$ is equivalent
to a category with a single object and a single morphism, i.e., the identity.
So in particular, the corresponding functor $D:\mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}\rightarrow
{\bf Ens}$ is a deformation functor.
\end{example}

The analogue of the Schlessinger conditions $(H_1)$,$(H_2)$ is the
Rim-Schlesssinger condition (RS), see \cite[Tag 06J3]{Stacks}. 
We say $\mathcal{D}$ satisfies (RS) if for ever diagram in $\mathcal{D}$
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:empty square}
\xymatrix@C=20pt
{
&X_{A_2}\ar[d]\\
X_{A_1}\ar[r]&X_A
}
\end{equation}
lying over
\[
\xymatrix@C=20pt
{
&A_2\ar[d]\\
A_1\ar[r]&A
}
\]
in $\mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}$ with $A_2\rightarrow A$ surjective, there exists
a fiber product $X_{A_1}\times_{X_A} X_{A_2}$ in $\mathcal{D}$ such that the
diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=20pt
{
X_{A_1}\times_{X_A} X_{A_2}\ar[r]\ar[d]&X_{A_2}\ar[d]\\
X_{A_1}\ar[r]&X_A
}
\]
lies over
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:full square}
\xymatrix@C=20pt
{
A_1\times_A A_2\ar[r]\ar[d]&A_2\ar[d]\\
A_1\ar[r]&A
}
\end{equation}

\begin{remark}
\label{rem:06J3}
We note from \cite[Tag~06J3]{Stacks} that if $\mathcal{D}$ satisfies (RS)
and $A_2\rightarrow A$ is surjective, then any commutative square
completing \eqref{eq:empty square} and lying over \eqref{eq:full square}
is a fibre square.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}
Example~\ref{ex:principal} satisfies condition (RS), with
\[
(X_{A_1},\mathcal{O}_{X_{A_1}})\times_{(X_A,\mathcal{O}_{X_A})} (X_{A_2},\mathcal{O}_{X_{A_2}})
=(X, \mathcal{O}_{X_{A_1}}\times_{\mathcal{O}_{X_A}} \mathcal{O}_{X_{A_2}}).
\]
\end{example}

                                                                                     
                                                                        
                                                                              
             
                                                                                 
                                                                           
                                                                            
Following \cite{KawaErr}, one may define $T^1(X_n/A_n)$ in this more
general context. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a predeformation category satisfying
(RS) and $X_n$
an object of $\mathcal{D}(A_n)$. Then $T^1(X_n/A_n)$ is defined to be
the set of isomorphism classes of pairs $(Y_n,\psi_n)$ consisting
an object $Y_n\in \mathcal{D}(B_n)$ and a morphism
$\psi_n:Y_n \rightarrow X_n$ over $\beta_n:B_n\rightarrow A_n$.  

Similarly to \ref{(1.5)}, $T^1(X_n/A_n)$
has a natural $A_n$-module structure. Indeed, given $(Y_n,\psi_n),
(Y_n',\psi_n')\in T^1(X_n/A_n)$, $Y_n\times_{X_n} Y_n'$ is well-defined
up to isomorphism in $\mathcal{D}(B_n\times_{A_n} B_n)$. Here the two maps
$Y_n,Y_n'\rightarrow X_n$ used to define the fibre product are $\psi_n$ and
$\psi'_n$ respectively.

The natural map $s:B_n\times_{A_n} B_n
\rightarrow B_n$ as before then yields an object $Y_n''=
s_*(Y_n\times_{X_n} Y_n')$ of $\mathcal{D}(B_n)$.
Further, $Y_n\times_{X_n} Y_n'$ carries a well-defined morphism to $X_n$,
so $Y_n''$ does also by the cofibred category property, see condition
(2) of \cite[Tag 06GJ]{Stacks}.
Multiplication by elements of $A_n$, is accomplished in the
same way as in \ref{(1.4)}.

body_md:
\label{(1.7)} 
If $D$ is a deformation functor on ${\bf C}_{\Lambda}$, we say that a
$k$-vector space $T^2$ is an obstruction space for $D$ if
whenever we have a surjection $\phi:A'\rightarrow A$
in ${\bf C}_{\Lambda}$ with $I=\operatorname{ker}\phi$ annihilated by the maximal ideal of $A'$, 
we get a sequence
\[
\xymatrix@C=20pt
{
D(A')\ar[r]^{D(\phi)}& D(A) \ar[r]^{\delta}& T^2\otimes I,
}
\]
and this sequence is exact in the sense that if
$\alpha\in D(A)$, then 
$\delta(\alpha)=0$ if and only if $\alpha$ is in the image
of $D(\phi)$. Furthermore, the obstruction map should be functorial, so given in
addition $\phi':B'\rightarrow B$ surjective, $I'=\operatorname{ker}\phi'$ annihilated by the
maximal ideal of $B'$ and a commutative diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=20pt
{
A'\ar[r]^{\phi}\ar[d]_{\beta'}&A\ar[d]^{\beta}\\
B'\ar[r]_{\phi'}&B
}
\]
there is a commutative diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=20pt
{D(A')\ar[r]^{D(\phi)}\ar[d]_{D(\beta')}&D(A)\ar[r]^{\delta}\ar[d]_{D(\beta)}
&T^2\otimes I\ar[d]^{1_{T^2}\otimes\beta'}\\
D(B')\ar[r]_{D(\phi')}&D(B)\ar[r]_{\delta'}
&T^2\otimes I'}
\]

If $D$ is prorepresentable by $S\cong R/J$ as in \ref{(1.2)}, it is easy to describe the
obstruction theory of
$D$. Let $T^2$ be the $k$-vector space $(J/{\bf m}_RJ)^{\vee}$. 
The obstruction map $\delta$ can be described as follows.
Given $f\in D(A)=\operatorname{Hom}(R/J,A)$, let $f(x_i)=\alpha_i\in A$. Choose any
lifting of $\alpha_i$ to $\alpha_i'\in A'$; this defines a $\Lambda$-algebra
homomorphism
$f':R\rightarrow A'$. Now given an element $\beta\in J$, we must have $f'(\beta)\in
I$, since
$f(\beta)=0$. Furthermore, if $\beta\in {\bf m}_RJ$, then $f'(\beta)=0$, since
$f'$ is a local homomorphism and $I$ is annihilated by the maximal ideal of $A'$. 
Thus
$f'$ induces a
$k$-vector space map
$J/{\bf m}_RJ\rightarrow I$, i.e. an element of $T^2\otimes I$. We then define
$\delta(f)$ to be this element. It is easy to see that $\delta(f)$ does not depend
on the choice of the lifting. Furthermore, it is clear that $f'$ induces a map
$f':R/J\rightarrow A'$ if and only if $\delta(f)=0$. Note that if one choice of the $\alpha_i'$ 
provides a lifting $f':R/J\rightarrow A'$, then
any choice does, and the set of possible liftings is a principal homogeneous space
over the vector space $(\mathfrak{m}_R/(\mathfrak{m}_{\Lambda}R+\mathfrak{m}_R^2))^{\vee}\otimes I$. 
 
We note also that $(J/{\bf m}_RJ)^{\vee}$ is naturally isomorphic to $T^1(S/\Lambda,
k)$ by \cite[3.1.2]{[25]}, where here $T^1$ is the first cotangent functor of Lichtenbaum
and Schlessinger.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{1.8}
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic 0, $\mathcal{D}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}_{k}$
a predeformation category satisfying (RS), 
$D$ the the corresponding deformation functor. Suppose that $D$
has an obstruction space $T^2$. Then for each
$X_n\in \mathcal{D}(A_n)$, $X_{n-1}=\alpha_{n-1,*}X_n$, let 
$\alpha\in T^1(X_{n-1}/A_{n-1})$
be given by the pair $(\epsilon_{n-1,*}X_n, \psi_{n-1})$ where 
$\psi_{n-1}$ is the canonical morphism 
$\epsilon_{n-1,*}X_n\rightarrow X_{n-1}$ guaranteed by 
\eqref{eq:pushfoward property}.
Then there exists an
$X_{n+1}\in D(A_{n+1})$ with $D(\alpha_n)(X_{n+1})=X_n$ if and only if $\alpha$ is in the image
of the natural map
$$\xi_{n*}:T^1(X_n/A_n)\rightarrow T^1(X_{n-1}/A_{n-1}).$$

name: Ran,Kawamata

title: Proof
body_md:
This proof is simply a very minor modification of Kawamata's proof
of Ran's $T^1$-lifting criterion in \cite{[18]}. 

First, the map $\xi_{n*}$ is defined as follows. An element of
$(Y_n,\psi_n)$ of $T^1(X_n/A_n)$ induces a composed map
$Y_n\rightarrow X_n\rightarrow \alpha_{n-1,*}X_n=X_{n-1}$, and hence
a morphism $\psi_{n-1}:Y_{n-1}:=\xi_{n*}Y_n\rightarrow X_{n-1}$ by
\eqref{eq:pushfoward property}.

As in \cite[pg.~185]{[18]}, we have
a commutative diagram with exact rows: 
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
D(A_{n+1})\ar[r]^{D(\alpha_n)}
\ar[d]_{D(\epsilon_n)}
&D(A_n)\ar[r]^{\delta_1}
\ar[d]_{D(\epsilon_{n}')}
&T^2\otimes (t^{n+1})
\ar[d]^{1_{T^2}\otimes
\epsilon_n}\\ 
D(B_n)\ar[r]_{D(\gamma_n)}&D(C_n)\ar[r]_{\delta_2}
&T^2\otimes (x^ny)}
\]
Note that $1_{T^2}\otimes\epsilon_n$ is an isomorphism 
(here we need $\operatorname{char} k=0$, since $\epsilon_n(t^{n+1})=(n+1)x^ny$ in $B_n$).

Put $Y_{n-1}:=\epsilon_{n-1,*}X_n$, so $\alpha=(Y_{n-1},\psi_{n-1})$.
Note that we have a commutative diagram, again using 
\eqref{eq:pushfoward property},
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
\epsilon_{n*}'X_n\ar[r]\ar[d]& \operatorname{pr}_{2*}\epsilon_{n*}'X_n=X_n\ar[d]\\
Y_{n-1}=\epsilon_{n-1,*}X_n\ar[r]_{\psi_{n-1}}&X_{n-1}=\alpha_{n-1,*}X_n
}
\]
sitting over the fibre square defining $C_n=B_{n-1}\times_{A_{n-1}} A_n$.
Here 
\[
\operatorname{pr}_2:B_{n-1}\times_{A_{n-1}} A_n\rightarrow A_n
\]
denotes the second projection.
Thus by Remark~\ref{rem:06J3}, $\epsilon_{n*}'X_n \cong 
Y_n\times_{X_{n-1}} X_n$.
Now
\begin{itemize}
\item[] $\exists X_{n+1}\in D(A_{n+1})$ such that $D(\alpha_n)(X_{n+1})=X_n$
\item[$\Leftrightarrow$]$\delta_1(X_n)=0$
\item[$\Leftrightarrow$]$\delta_2(D(\epsilon'_n)(X_n))=0$
\item[$\Leftrightarrow$]$\exists Y_n\in D(B_n)$ with
$D(\gamma_n)(Y_n)=D(\epsilon_n')(X_n)$
\item[$\Leftrightarrow$]$\exists$ an object $Y_n$ in $\mathcal{D}(B_n)$
fitting into a commutative diagram 
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
\gamma_{n*}Y_n\ar[r]\ar[d] & X_n\ar[d]\\
Y_{n-1}\ar[r]_{\psi_{n-1}}&X_{n-1}
}
\]
sitting over the fibre square defining
$B_{n-1}\times_{A_{n-1}} A_n$ 
\item[$\Leftrightarrow$]$\exists$ $Y_n$ an object of $\mathcal{D}(B_n)$
with morphisms
$\psi_n:Y_n\rightarrow X_n$ over $\beta_n$ and $\phi:Y_n\rightarrow
Y_{n-1}$ over $\xi_n$ yielding a commutative diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
Y_n\ar[r]^{\psi_n}\ar[d]_{\phi}&X_n\ar[d]\\
Y_{n-1}\ar[r]_{\psi_{n-1}}&X_{n-1}
}
\]
(Here, we use $\xi_n$ is the composition $\operatorname{pr}_1\circ\gamma_n$ where
\[
\operatorname{pr}_1:C_n=B_{n-1}\times_{A_{n-1}} A_n\rightarrow B_{n-1}
\]
is the first projection, as well as properties of cofibred categories.)
\item[$\Leftrightarrow$]$\exists\alpha'\in T^1(X_n/A_n)$ mapping to $\alpha$.
\end{itemize}

label: def:predef functor
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:predef functor}
Let $p_i:\mathcal{D}_i\rightarrow \mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}$ be two predeformation categories.
A functor $F:\mathcal{D}_1\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_2$ is \emph{functor of predeformation 
categories} if $p_2\circ F=p_1$ and $F(\alpha_* X)=\alpha_*F(X)$ for
every $\alpha:A\rightarrow B$ in $\mathcal{C}_{\Lambda}$ and $X$ an object in
$\mathcal{D}_1(A)$.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{1.9}
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed\footnote{This hypothesis is
added as in \cite{KawaErr}.} field of characteristic 0, $\mathcal{D}_1,\mathcal{D}_2
\rightarrow {\bf C}_k$ two predeformation categories
with a functor of predeformation categories $F:\mathcal{D}_1\rightarrow
\mathcal{D}_2$. Suppose $D_1$ is pro-representable by a $k$-algebra $S\cong P/I$, 
$P=k[[x_1,\ldots,x_s]]$ as in \ref{(1.2)}. Suppose $\mathcal{D}_2$
satisfies condition (RS) and
$D_2$ has a hull $\Lambda$. Let $T^2_1$ and
$T^2_2$ be $k$-vector spaces and $l:T^2_1
\rightarrow T^2_2$ a $k$-vector space map. Denote by
$X$ a representative of the unique isomorphism class
of object of $\mathcal{D}_1(k)$. Suppose, for all $n$ and for each object
$X_n$ of $\mathcal{D}_1(A_n)$ inducing an object $X_{n-1}:=\xi_{n*}X_n$ of
$D_1(A_{n-1})$, there is a commutative diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
T^1_1(X_n/A_n)\ar[r]^{F_*}
\ar[d]_{\xi_{n*}}
&T^1_2(F(X_n)/A_n)
\ar[d]^{\xi_{n*}}\\
T^1_1(X_{n-1}/A_{n-1})\ar[r]_{F_*}
\ar[d]_{\delta_1}
&T^1_2(F(X_{n-1})/A_{n-1})
\ar[d]^{\delta_2}\\
T^2_1\ar[r]_{l}&T^2_2
}
\]

injective and where $F_*(Y_n,\psi_n)$ is $(F(Y_n),F(\psi_n))$. Then

\[
r=\dim_k\operatorname{ker}(T_1^1(X/k)\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{F_*}} T^1_2(F(X)/k)),

and $J\subseteq
\mathfrak{m}_{\Lambda}R+\mathfrak{m}_R^2$ an ideal. In addition, there is an ideal

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\Lambda$ is a hull for $D_2$, there is an induced map
$\Lambda\rightarrow S$, unique only up to the induced map $F_*$ on Zariski tangent
spaces. Fix one such map. Now
$$r=\dim_k \operatorname{coker}(\mathfrak{m}_{\Lambda}/\mathfrak{m}_{\Lambda}^2\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{{F_*}^{\vee}}}\mathfrak{m}_S/\mathfrak{m}_S^2),$$
and if we choose elements $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\in \mathfrak{m}_S$ which along with
$\operatorname{im}{F_*}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}$ generate $\mathfrak{m}_S/\mathfrak{m}_S^2$, we can define a map
$R=\Lambda[[x_1,\ldots,x_r]]
\rightarrow S$ by $x_i\mapsto \alpha_i$. This map is surjective, and if its kernel
is $J$, $S\cong R/J$. Furthermore, $J\subseteq\mathfrak{m}_{\Lambda}R+\mathfrak{m}_R^2$. Let $D_0:
{\bf C}_{\Lambda}\rightarrow {\bf Ens}$ be the functor pro-represented by 
the complete local $\Lambda$-algebra $S=R/J$.
We will first prove:

\begin{claim}
\label{(1.10)} If $V=\operatorname{coker}(T^1_1(X/k)\rightarrow
T^1_2(F(X)/k))$, then $V\subseteq {(J/\mathfrak{m}_RJ)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}$, and the obstruction map 
$\delta_0$ in
$$D_0(A_{n+1})\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}} D_0(A_n)\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\delta_0}} {(J/\mathfrak{m}_RJ)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\otimes
(t^{n+1})$$ always takes its values in $V\otimes (t^{n+1})$. 
\end{claim}


\begin{proof}
First note the change of rings sequence for the functors
$T^i$ of Lichtenbaum and Schlessinger (\cite[2.3.5]{[25]})
for
$k\rightarrow\Lambda\rightarrow S$
yields the exact sequence
$$T^0(S/k,k)\rightarrow T^0(\Lambda/k,k) \rightarrow T^1(S/\Lambda,k)
\rightarrow T^1(S/k,k),$$
or equivalently
\begin{equation}
\label{(1.11)}
{({\bf m}_S/{\bf m}^2_S)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\rightarrow {({\bf m}_{\Lambda}/{\bf
m}^2_{\Lambda})}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee} \rightarrow
{(J/\mathfrak{m}_RJ)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{d}} {(I/\mathfrak{m}_PI)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}.\
\end{equation}
Thus $\operatorname{ker} d=V$. Furthermore, the map $d$ is compatible with the obstruction maps.
Specifically, fixing a $\Lambda$-algebra structure on $A_{n+1}$,
hence inducing one on $A_n$, we obtain the diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{D_0(A_{n+1})\ar[r]\ar[d]&D_1(A_{n+1})\ar[d]\\
D_0(A_n)\ar[r]\ar[d]_{\delta_0}&D_1(A_n)\ar[d]_{\delta_1'}\\
{(J/\mathfrak{m}_RJ)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\otimes (t^{n+1})\ar[r]_{d\otimes 1}&{(I/\mathfrak{m}_PI)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\otimes
(t^{n+1})
}
\]
where the top two horizontal maps are the forgetful inclusions
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda-alg}(R/J,A_i)\subseteq
\operatorname{Hom}_{k-alg}(R/J,A_i)$ for $i=n+1,n$.
This is commutative for all $n$.

Since $\Lambda$ is a hull for $D_2$,
the compatible $\Lambda$-algebra structures on $A_{n+1},A_n,A_{n-1}$ induce
elements
$X_i'\in D_2(A_i)$, for $i=n-1,n$ and $n+1$. We may choose an object of
$\mathcal{D}_2(A_{n+1})$ representing $X'_{n+1}$, which we also write as
$X'_{n+1}$, so that we have representatives $X_n'=\alpha_{n,*}X_{n+1}'$
and $X_{n-1}'=\alpha_{n-1,*}X_n'$. 

Let
$X_n\in D_0(A_n)\subseteq D_1(A_n)$ be arbitrary, so that $F(X_n)=X_n'$ as
elements of $D_2(A_n)$. Choosing a representative of the isomorphism class
of $X_n$, also written as $X_n$, we obtain an isomorphism 
$X_n'\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\cong}} F(X_n)$
in $\mathcal{D}_2(A_n)$. Let $X_{n-1}=\alpha_{n-1,*}X_n$, 
$\psi_{n-1}:\epsilon_{n-1,*}X_n\rightarrow X_{n-1}$ the natural map
as in Theorem~\ref{1.8}. 
Let $v_{n-1}\in T^1_1(X_{n-1}/A_{n-1})$ be given by the pair
$(\epsilon_{n-1,*}X_n,\psi_{n-1})$. This gives 
$v'_{n-1}=F_*(v_{n-1})\in T^1_2(F(X_{n-1})/A_{n-1})$.

The isomorphism $X_{n-1}'\cong F(X_{n-1})$ induces a canonical isomorphism
\[
T^1_2(F(X_{n-1})/A_{n-1})\cong T^1_2(X_{n-1}'/A_{n-1})
\]
given by 
\[
(Y_{n-1}, Y_{n-1}\rightarrow F(X_{n-1}))\mapsto
(Y_{n-1}\times_{F(X_{n-1})} X_{n-1}',Y_{n-1}\times_{F(X_{n-1})} X_{n-1}'
\rightarrow X_{n-1}'),
\]
the fibre product existing by the (RS) condition. On the other hand,
by the co-fibred property,
we have a commutative diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=20pt
{
X'_n\ar[r]^{\cong}\ar[d]& F(X_n)\ar[d]\\
\alpha_{n-1,*}X'_n\ar[r]_{\cong}& \alpha_{n-1,*}F(X_n)
}
\]
and hence a commutative diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=20pt
{
\epsilon_{n-1,*}X'_n\ar[r]^{\cong}\ar[d]& \epsilon_{n-1,*}F(X_n)\ar[d]\\
\alpha_{n-1,*}X'_n\ar[r]_{\cong}& \alpha_{n-1,*}F(X_n)
}
\]
Using Definition~\ref{def:predef functor}, this diagram is the same
as
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
\epsilon_{n-1,*}X'_n\ar[r]\ar[d]&
F(\epsilon_{n-1,*}X_n)\ar[d]\\
X_{n-1}'\ar[r]& F(X_{n-1})
}
\]
Thus by Remark~\ref{rem:06J3}, this is a fibre diagram, and so
$v_{n-1}'\in T^1_2(F(X_{n-1}/A_{n-1}))$ is identified with
$v''_{n-1}=(\epsilon_{n-1,*}X'_n, \epsilon_{n-1,*}X'_n\rightarrow X'_{n-1})
\in T^1_2(X'_{n-1}/A_{n-1})$. Since $X_{n+1}'$ is a lifting of $X_n'$,
we see by Theorem \ref{1.8} that $v_{n-1}''$ is in the image of 
$T^1_2(X'_n/A_n)\rightarrow T^1_2(X'_{n-1}/A_{n-1})$, and hence
$v_{n-1}'$ is in the image of 
$T^1_2(F(X_n)/A_n)\rightarrow T^1_2(F(X_{n-1})/A_{n-1})$. 
Thus $\delta_2(v_{n-1}')=0$.  Since
$l|_{\operatorname{im}(\delta_1)}$ is injective, $\delta_1(v_{n-1})=0$. Again by Theorem \ref{1.8},
$X_n$ lifts to
$X_{n+1}\in D_1(A_{n+1})$, so $(d\otimes 1)\circ \delta_0(X_n)=\delta_1'(X_n)=0$, so
$\delta_0(X_n)\in\operatorname{ker} d\otimes 1= V\otimes (t^{n+1})$. Thus the image of $\delta_0$
is contained in
$V\otimes (t^{n+1})$. This proves the claim.
\end{proof}

We now follow some of the ideas of Kawamata in \cite{[19]} to construct $J'$. Dualizing
the sequence \eqref{(1.11)}, we have
$$J/\mathfrak{m}_RJ\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\phi}} \mathfrak{m}_{\Lambda}/\mathfrak{m}^2_{\Lambda} \smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{{F_*}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}}}
\mathfrak{m}_S/\mathfrak{m}_S^2.$$
Let $f_1,\ldots, f_t\in J$ be elements such that $\phi(f_1),\ldots,\phi(f_t)$
generate $\operatorname{ker} {F_*}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}$, with $t=\dim_k \operatorname{ker} {F_*}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}=\dim_k V$. Set $J'
=(f_1,\ldots,f_t)$. There is a surjective map
$\mathfrak{m}_R/(\mathfrak{m}_R^2+J')\rightarrow \mathfrak{m}_R/(\mathfrak{m}_R^2+J)$ and the dimensions of these spaces
are
the same by construction, so we have equality. 

The map 
$J'/\mathfrak{m}_RJ'\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{i}} J/\mathfrak{m}_RJ$ induced by $J'\subseteq J$ is an inclusion since
\[
\dim_k J'/\mathfrak{m}_RJ'\le t
\]
but $\dim_k \operatorname{im}(\phi\circ i)=t$. Thus
dually the composition
$$V\rightarrow {(J/\mathfrak{m}_RJ)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee} \rightarrow {(J'/\mathfrak{m}_RJ')}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}$$
is an isomorphism. Let $D_0':{\bf C}_{\Lambda}\rightarrow {\bf Ens}$ be the functor
pro-represented by $R/J'$. Clearly $D_0$ is a subfunctor of $D_0'$, and for each
$n$, we have a commutative diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{D_0(A_{n+1})\ar[r]\ar[d]&D_0(A_n)\ar[r]^{\delta_0}\ar[d]& V\otimes
(t^{n+1})\ar[d]^{\cong}\\
D_0'(A_{n+1})\ar[r]&D_0'(A_n)\ar[r]_{\delta_0'}&{(J'/\mathfrak{m}_RJ')}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\otimes
(t^{n+1})
}
\]
This shows that an element of $D_0(A_n)$ lifts to $D_0(A_{n+1})$ if and only if
it lifts to $D_0'(A_{n+1})$. Since the choice of liftings is a principal
homogeneous space over ${(\mathfrak{m}_R/(\mathfrak{m}_R\Lambda+\mathfrak{m}_R^2))}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\otimes (t^{n+1})$ for
both $D_0$ and $D_0'$, we see inductively that
$D_0(A_n) =D_0'(A_n)$ for any $\Lambda$-algebra structure on $A_n$. Thus
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda-alg}(R/J,k[[t]])=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda-alg}(R/J',k[[t]])$$
for any $\Lambda$-algebra structure on $k[[t]]$, and so
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{k-alg}(R/J,k[[t]])=\operatorname{Hom}_{k-alg}(R/J',k[[t]])$$
and we conclude that $\operatorname{Supp}(R/J)=\operatorname{Supp}(R/J')$ as in the last paragraph of the proof
of \cite[Thm.~1]{[19]}.\footnote{This is where the added hypothesis that
$k$ is algebraically closed is necessary.}

\label{(2.1)}
Let $X$ be a Calabi-Yau threefold with canonical singularities over $k=\mathbb{C}$,
the complex numbers, i.e., a projective threefold with canonical singularities,
$K_{X}=0$, and $h^1(\mathcal{O}_{X})=0$. Set $Z=\operatorname{Sing}(X)$. Note $Z$ can be zero or one dimensional.
We want to study the deformation
theory of
$X$. In particular, we will relate the deformation theory of $X$ to the deformation
theory of $\hat X$, the formal completion of $X$ along $Z$. To paraphrase Theorem
\ref{2.2} below, we will find that the obstructions to deforming $X$ are contained in the
obstructions to deforming $\hat X$, i.e. ``obstructions to deforming $X$ are local
to the singularities of $X$.''

To make this concept rigorous, let $D$ be the functor of deformations of $X$, 
and let $D_{\mathrm{loc}}$ be the functor of deformations of $\hat X$, as in 
Example~\ref{ex:principal}. There
is a natural morphism of functors $F:D\rightarrow D_{\mathrm{loc}}$ taking a deformation
to its completion along $Z$. Note that $D$ is pro-representable
since
$\operatorname{Hom}(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_X)=0$ by \cite[Cor.~8.6]{[17]}.

If $X_n$ is a deformation of
$X$ over $A_n$, we have
$T^1(X_n/A_n)\cong
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_n})$ and $T^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X_n/A_n)\cong
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n}\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}} \mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n},
\mathcal{O}_{\hat
X_n})$. The former isomorphism is well-known. For the latter, if $X_n/A_n$
is locally embedded in $Y_n/A_n$ smooth with ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}$, then the local
${\bf T}^1$ sheaf of $\hat X_n/A_n$ is as usual given by
$$\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}}(\Omega^1_{\hat Y_n/A_n}|_{\hat X_n}, \mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n})
\rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}}(\widehat{\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2}, \mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n})\rightarrow
{\bf T}^1\rightarrow 0.$$
Note that $\Omega^1_{Y_n/A_n}\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{Y_n}} \mathcal{O}_{\hat Y_n} \cong
\hat\Omega^1_{\hat Y_n/A_n}$, the completion of $\Omega^1_{\hat Y_n/A_n}$
(see \cite[Chap.~0, 20.7.14]{[14]}). Since $\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}$ is complete, 
\begin{align*}
\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}}(\Omega^1_{\hat Y_n/A_n}|_{\hat X_n}, \mathcal{O}_{\hat
X_n})= {} &
\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}}(\hat\Omega^1_{\hat Y_n/A_n}|_{\hat X_n}, \mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n})\\
={} &
\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}}(\Omega^1_{Y_n/A_n}|_{X_n}\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}
\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}, \mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}).
\end{align*}
Thus from the exact sequence
$$\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}} \mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}\rightarrow \Omega^1_{Y_n/A_n}|_{X_n}\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}
\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n} \rightarrow \Omega^1_{X_n/A_n}\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}} \mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}
\rightarrow 0$$
we see that ${\bf T}^1\cong \underline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1_{\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n}
\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}} \mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n},
\mathcal{O}_{\hat
X_n})$. Local infinitesimal deformations of $\hat X_n$ then patch together as usual
to yield an element of
$\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n}\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}} \mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n},
\mathcal{O}_{\hat
X_n})$.

Finally, let $T^2=\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\Omega^1_X, \mathcal{O}_X)$ and $T^2_{\mathrm{loc}}=\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{O}_{X}}
(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_{\hat X})$. Let $l:T^2\rightarrow T^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ be the map induced
by the map $\mathcal{O}_X\rightarrow\mathcal{O}_{\hat X}$.

body_md:
\label{2.3} 
Given the hypotheses of \ref{(2.1)}, if $X_n$ is a deformation
of $X$ over $A_n$, then there are natural isomorphisms 
$$\operatorname{Ext}^i_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_m})\cong
\operatorname{Ext}^i_{\mathcal{O}_{X_m}}(\Omega^1_{X_m/A_m},\mathcal{O}_{X_m})$$
for $m<n, i\le 2$ and $X_m=X_n\otimes_{A_n} A_m$.

title: Proof
body_md:
The change of rings spectral sequence (\cite[Thm.~10.74]{[40]}) tells us that
$$\underline{\operatorname{Ext}}^p_{\mathcal{O}_{X_m}}({\rm Tor}^{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}_q(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_m}),\mathcal{O}_{X_m})
\Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{Ext}}^i_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_m}).$$
Now $\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n}$ is a flat $\mathcal{O}_{X_n}$-module away from $Z\subseteq X_n$, so
${\rm Tor}^{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}_q(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_m})$ is supported on $Z$ for $q\ge 1$.
Since $X_m$ is Cohen-Macaulay,
\[
\underline{\operatorname{Ext}}^p_{\mathcal{O}_{X_m}}({\rm Tor}^{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}_q(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_m}),\mathcal{O}_{X_m})=0
\]
for $p\le 1, q\ge 1$. Thus
\begin{align*}
\underline{\operatorname{Ext}}^i_{\mathcal{O}_{X_m}}(\Omega^1_{X_m/A_m},\mathcal{O}_{X_m})= {} &
\underline{\operatorname{Ext}}^i_{\mathcal{O}_{X_m}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n}\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}\mathcal{O}_{X_m},\mathcal{O}_{X_m})\\
={} & \underline{\operatorname{Ext}}^i_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_m})
\end{align*}
for $i\le 2$. The statement of the lemma for global Exts then follows from the
local-global spectral sequence for Exts.

body_md:
The change of rings spectral sequence yields
$$\underline{\operatorname{Ext}}^p_{\mathcal{O}_{X_m}}({\rm Tor}^{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}_q(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_m}),\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_m})
\Rightarrow \underline{\operatorname{Ext}}^i_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_m}),$$
so the same argument as in the proof of Lemma \ref{2.3} shows that
$$\operatorname{Ext}^i_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_m})\cong
\operatorname{Ext}^i_{\mathcal{O}_{X_m}}(\Omega^1_{X_m/A_m},\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_m})$$
for $i\le 2$. Furthermore, since $\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_m}$
is a flat $\mathcal{O}_{X_m}$-module,
$$\operatorname{Ext}^i_{\mathcal{O}_{X_m}}(\Omega^1_{X_m/A_m},\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_m})
\cong\operatorname{Ext}^i_{\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_m}}(\Omega^1_{X_m/A_m}\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{X_m}} \mathcal{O}_{\hat X_m},
\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_m}),$$ which is $T^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X_m/A_m)$ by \ref{(2.1)} for $i=1$.
For $i=2$, $m=0$, this gives (b).

(c) follows from the usual statement of local
duality if $Z$ is dimension zero. Since $X$ may not have isolated singularities, 
we use Alonso, Jerem\'\i as and Lipman's generalization of local
duality \cite{[1]}. By \cite[(0.3), (0.1), and (0.4.1)]{[1]}, 
$${\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{O}_X}({\bf R}{\underline\Gamma}_Z\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_X)
\cong{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_{\hat X}).$$
By the Grothendieck duality theorem of \cite{[15]}, 
\begin{align*}
{\bf R}\Gamma{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{O}_X}({\bf
R}{\underline\Gamma}_Z\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_X)\cong {} & \operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}_k({\bf R}\Gamma{\bf
R}{\underline\Gamma}_Z\Omega^1_X,k[-3])\\
= {} &\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}_k({\bf R}\Gamma_Z\Omega^1_X,k[-3]).
\end{align*}
Putting these two isomorphisms together and taking cohomology of the two complexes,
we have
$$H^i(\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}_k({\bf R}\Gamma_Z\Omega^1_X,k[-3]))\cong H^i({\bf
R}\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_{\hat X})).$$
For $i=2$, this yields the isomorphism
$${(H^1_Z(\Omega^1_X))}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\cong \operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_{\hat X})\cong
T^2_{\mathrm{loc}}.$$
This isomorphism is compatible with the map
\[
T^2=\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_X)\rightarrow
\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_{\hat X})=T^2_{\mathrm{loc}}
\]
induced by the map $\mathcal{O}_X\rightarrow
\mathcal{O}_{\hat X}$ since \cite[(0.3)]{[1]} also tells us that the following diagram is
commutative:
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_X}^{\bullet}(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_X)
\ar[d]_{\alpha}\ar[rd]^{\beta}
&\\
{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{O}_X}({\bf R}{\underline\Gamma}_Z\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_X)
\ar[r]_{\cong}&{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^{\bullet}_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_{\hat X})
}
\]
where $\alpha$ is induced by the natural map in the derived category ${\bf
R}{\underline\Gamma}_Z\Omega^1_X
\rightarrow \Omega^1_X$ and $\beta$ is induced by $\mathcal{O}_X\rightarrow \mathcal{O}_{\hat X}$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{2.5} 
The image of the map 
$$d\log:H^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X^*)\rightarrow H^1(X,\tilde\Omega^1_X)$$
generates $H^1(X,\tilde\Omega_X^1)$ as a $k$-vector space.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof of \cite[Lem.~2.2]{[28]} actually shows in general that
the image of $H^1(X,\mathcal{O}_X^*)\rightarrow H^1(X,\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})$
generates the latter as a vector space, using only the hypothesis
that $\tilde X$ has rational singularities, which is true of any
canonical singularity. Now the kernel and cokernel of
$\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X}\rightarrow \tilde\Omega^1_X$ are supported on $Z$.
If we can show furthermore that $\operatorname{coker}(\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X}\rightarrow
\tilde \Omega^1_X)$ is supported on a finite set of points, then in fact
$H^1(\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^1(\tilde\Omega^1_X)$ is surjective
and the lemma follows. 

By \cite{[38]}, except for a finite number of dissident points,
$X$ is analytically isomorphic in a neighborhood of a point of $Z$ to 
$\Delta\times S$, where $\Delta$ is the germ of a curve and $S$ is a germ of
a du Val surface singularity, with resolution $\pi':\tilde S\rightarrow S$. Thus, in 
this neighborhood, $\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow X$ looks like $\pi:\Delta\times\tilde S
\rightarrow \Delta\times S$. Let $p_1$ and $p_2$ be the projections of
$\Delta\times S$ onto $\Delta$ and $S$ respectively. The map
$\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X}\rightarrow
\tilde \Omega^1_X$ is $p_1^*\Omega^1_{\Delta}\oplus p_2^*\pi'_*\Omega^1_{\tilde
S}\rightarrow
p_1^*\Omega^1_{\Delta}\oplus p_2^*\tilde\Omega^1_S$. Since $S$ is a rational
singularity,  it follows from \cite{[43]} that $\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde S}\rightarrow \tilde
\Omega^1_S$ is surjective. Thus $\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde
X}\rightarrow\tilde\Omega^1_X$ is surjective in this neighborhood, and so
$\operatorname{coker}(\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X}\rightarrow\tilde\Omega^1_X)$ is concentrated on the
dissident points of $Z$.

label: eq:ext sequence
title: Proof
body_md:
To obtain the first column of the diagram, we apply the functor
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\cdot)$ to the exact sequence
$$0\to\mathcal{O}_X\to\mathcal{O}_{X_n}\to\mathcal{O}_{X_{n-1}}\to0$$
yielding
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ext sequence}
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_n})\rightarrow
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_{n-1}})\rightarrow
\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_X),
\end{equation}
from which we obtain the first column, by Lemma \ref{2.3}.
The second column is obtained by
applying
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n},\cdot)$ to the sequence
$$0\to\mathcal{O}_{\hat X}\to\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}\to\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_{n-1}}\to0,$$ and applying
Lemma \ref{2.4}. The maps between the columns induced by the maps $\mathcal{O}_{X_n}\rightarrow
\mathcal{O}_{\hat X_n}$
yield a commutative diagram. For the first two rows, these maps coincide with
the maps induced by $F:D\rightarrow D_{\mathrm{loc}}$.

We now only need to
show that $l|_{\operatorname{im}(\delta)}:\operatorname{im}(\delta)\rightarrow T^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is injective for each
such diagram. This is equivalent to ${l|_{\operatorname{im}(\delta)}}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}:{(T^2_{\mathrm{loc}})}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}
\rightarrow {\operatorname{im}(\delta)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}$ being surjective. 

We have a diagram
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:big diagram}
\xymatrix@=30pt
{H^1_Z(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n})\ar[r]\ar[d]&H^1(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n})
\ar[r]\ar[d]&H^1(\tilde\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n})\ar[d]&\\
H^1_Z(\Omega^1_X)\ar[r]\ar[d]&H^1(\Omega^1_X)\ar[d]
\ar[r]&\ar[d]H^1(\tilde\Omega^1_X)\ar[d]&\\
K_{\mathrm{loc}}\ar[r]\ar[d]&K\ar[r]\ar[d]&0\\
0&0&
}
\end{equation}
Here the vertical
maps between the first two rows are induced by the restriction map
$\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n}\rightarrow \Omega^1_X$, and $K_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $K$ are
just defined to make the columns exact. The map $H^1_Z(\Omega^1_X)
\rightarrow H^1(\Omega^1_X)$ is dual to $l:T^2\rightarrow T^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$, by
Lemma \ref{2.4} (c). I claim the rows of this diagram are exact. 

{\it Exactness of the first two rows:} For any $n$, we have the exact sequence
$$0\rightarrow \mathbb{H}^0_Z(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n})\rightarrow \Omega^1_{X_n/A_n}
\rightarrow \tilde\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n} \rightarrow \mathbb{H}^1_Z(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n})
\rightarrow 0.$$
Now $\mathbb{H}^0_Z(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n})$ is supported on the set of points of $X$ which 
are not locally complete intersection, and so has finite support. Thus
$H^1(\mathbb{H}^0_Z(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n}))=0$ and $H^1_Z(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n})
=H^0(\mathbb{H}^1_Z(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n}))$. From this
follows exactness of the first two rows. 

{\it Exactness of the last row:} As in
\cite{[28]}, there is a diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
H^1(\mathcal{O}_{X_n}^*)\ar[d]_{\alpha}\ar[r]&H^1(\tilde\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n})\ar[d]\\
H^1(\mathcal{O}_X^*)\ar[r]&H^1(\tilde\Omega^1_X)
}
\]
with $\alpha$ surjective since $H^2(\mathcal{O}_X)=0$, and by Lemma \ref{2.5}, the image
of $H^1(\mathcal{O}_X^*)$ in $H^1(\tilde \Omega^1_X)$ generates the latter as a
$k$-vector space. Thus the composed map $H^1(\mathcal{O}_{X_n}^*)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k
\rightarrow H^1(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n})\rightarrow H^1(\tilde\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n})
\rightarrow H^1(\tilde\Omega^1_X)$ is surjective, and so the map 
$H^1(\Omega^1_{X_n/A_n})\rightarrow H^1(\tilde\Omega^1_X)$ is surjective.
Now a simple diagram chase shows that the last row is exact.

\medskip

The diagram \eqref{eq:big diagram} now shows that 
the composed map $H^1_Z(\Omega^1_X)\rightarrow K$ is surjective. 

We now consider the following isomorphisms of $\partial$-functors (i.e., these
functors take triangles to triangles and the isomorphisms preserve triangles):
\begin{align}
\label{key iso}
\begin{split}
{\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(Rf_*(\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L \bullet),A_n)
\cong {} &  {\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L \bullet, \omega_{X_n/A_n}[3])\\
\cong {} & {\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},
{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\bullet,\omega_{X_n/A_n}[3])),
\end{split}
\end{align}
where $f:X_n\rightarrow \operatorname{Spec} A_n$ is the structure morphism.
Here the first isomorphism is Grothendieck duality as stated in
\cite[Thm.~(4.1.1)]{Lip}, which also states it is a $\partial$-functor.
The second isomorphism is \cite[Prop.~5.15]{[15]} or \cite[Prop.~(2.6.1)]{Lip}.
Following \cite{[15]}, the first isomorphism
requires $\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L\bullet$ to lie in $D^-_{qc}(X_n)$,
i.e., complexes of quasicoherent sheaves bounded above,
and the second isomorphism requires $\bullet$ to lie in
$D^-_c(X)$, i.e., complexes of coherent sheaves bounded above.
We wish to apply this for $\bullet=\mathcal{O}_{X_m}$ for various $m\le n$.
Since this sheaf has a resolution by locally free sheaves
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:resolution}
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{\cdots\ar[r]&\mathcal{O}_{X_n}\ar[r]^{t^{m+1}}&\mathcal{O}_{X_n}\ar[r]^{t^{n-m}}&
\mathcal{O}_{X_n}\ar[r]^{t^{m+1}}&\mathcal{O}_{X_n}\ar[r]&\mathcal{O}_{X_{m}}\ar[r]&0,}
\end{equation}
$\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L \mathcal{O}_{X_m}$ is represented by a complex
bounded above, as needed. 

We apply these isomorphisms to the triangle arising from the exact sequence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:triangle}
0\rightarrow \mathcal{O}_{X_{n-1}} \rightarrow \mathcal{O}_{X_n}\rightarrow \mathcal{O}_X\rightarrow 0.
\end{equation}
Because these isomorphisms are isomorphisms of $\partial$-functors,
after taking cohomology of the left and right sides of \eqref{key iso},
we obtain isomorphic long exact sequences of
$A_n$-modules, the key part of these being, for us:
\begin{align}
\label{eq:exact1}
\begin{split}
&H^{-2}( {\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(Rf_*(\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L \mathcal{O}_{X_n}),A_n))\\
\rightarrow {} & 
H^{-2}({\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(Rf_*(\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L \mathcal{O}_{X_{n-1}}),A_n))\\
\rightarrow {} &H^{-1}({\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(Rf_*(\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L \mathcal{O}_X),A_n))
\end{split}
\end{align}
and 
\begin{align}
\label{eq:exact2}
\begin{split}
&H^{-2}({\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},
{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\mathcal{O}_{X_n},\omega_{X_n/A_n}[3])))\\
\rightarrow {} & 
H^{-2}({\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},
{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\mathcal{O}_{X_{n-1}},\omega_{X_n/A_n}[3])))\\
\rightarrow {} & H^{-1}({\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},
{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\mathcal{O}_X,\omega_{X_n/A_n}[3])))
\end{split}
\end{align}

Let us first compute the terms in \eqref{eq:exact1}. As $A_n$ is
an injective $A_n$-module, we may replace ${\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(\bullet,
A_n)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(\bullet,A_n)$. Thus \eqref{eq:exact1}
may be written as
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(\mathbb{H}^2(X_n,\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L \mathcal{O}_{X_{n}}),A_n)
& \rightarrow
\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(\mathbb{H}^2(X_n,\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L \mathcal{O}_{X_{n-1}}),A_n)\\ &
\rightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(\mathbb{H}^1(X_n,\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L \mathcal{O}_X),A_n).
\end{align*}
As $\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L \mathcal{O}_{X_n}\cong \Omega_{X_n/A_n}$, the first
term is just $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(H^2(X_n,\Omega_{X_n/A_n}),A_n)$. The other
two terms can be computed via the hypercohomology spectral sequence
(for $m=n-1$ or $0$) given at the $E^2$ term by
\[
H^p(X_n,\mathcal{H}^q(\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L\mathcal{O}_{X_m}))
\Rightarrow \mathbb{H}^{p+q}(X_n,\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L\mathcal{O}_{X_m}),
\]
where $\mathcal{H}^*$ denotes cohomology of a complex of sheaves.
Now 
\[
\mathcal{H}^q(\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L\mathcal{O}_{X_m})=\operatorname{Tor}_{-q}^{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}
(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_m}).
\]
The latter is $\Omega_{X_m/A_m}$ for
$q=0$ and is supported on $\operatorname{Sing}(X)$ for $q<0$. Thus
the spectral sequence is fourth quadrant and
has the following terms, the upper left entry
being the $(0,0)$ entry:
\[
\begin{matrix}
H^0(X_n,\Omega_{X_m/A_m})&
H^1(X_n,\Omega_{X_m/A_m})&
H^2(X_n,\Omega_{X_m/A_m})&
H^3(X_n,\Omega_{X_m/A_m})\\
?&?&0&0\\
?&?&0&0
\end{matrix}
\]
The spectral sequence thus degenerates at the $E_2$ term, and one
sees that
\[
\mathbb{H}^i(X_n,\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L\mathcal{O}_{X_m})
\cong H^i(X_n,\Omega_{X_m/A_m})=H^i(X_m,\Omega_{X_m/A_m})
\]
for $i=1,2$.
In particular, the long exact sequence of hypercohomology obtained by
applying the functor $\mathbb{H}^{\bullet}(X_n,\Omega_{X_n/A_n}\otimes^L \bullet)$
to the triangle obtained from \eqref{eq:triangle} produces the long
exact sequence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:second long}
H^1(\Omega_{X_n/A_n})\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}} H^1(\Omega_X)
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}} H^2(\Omega_{X_{n-1}/A_{n-1}}) \smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\cdot t}}
H^2(\Omega_{X_n/A_n})
\end{equation}
showing that 
\[
K=\operatorname{ker}(H^2(\Omega_{X_{n-1}/A_{n-1}})
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\cdot t}} H^2(\Omega_{X_n/A_n}))
=\operatorname{im}(H^1(\Omega_X)\rightarrow H^2(\Omega_{X_n/A_n})).
\]
Also, noting that $\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(M,A_n)=\operatorname{Hom}_{A_m}(M,A_m)$ for $M$ an $A_m$-module,
we get that \eqref{eq:exact1} coincides with
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dual sequence}
\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(H^2(\Omega_{X_n/A_n}),A_n)
\rightarrow
\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{n-1}}(H^2(\Omega_{X_{n-1}/A_{n-1}}),A_{n-1})
\rightarrow
\operatorname{Hom}_k(H^1(\Omega_{X/k}),k),
\end{equation}
the dual of the last three terms of \eqref{eq:second long}.

We turn to \eqref{eq:exact2}. We 
calculate for $m\le n$, and $i=-2,-1$:
\begin{align*}
&H^{i}({\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},
{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\mathcal{O}_{X_m},\omega_{X_n/A_n}[3])))\\
\cong {} &
H^{i+3}({\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},
{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\mathcal{O}_{X_m},\omega_{X_n/A_n})))\\
\cong {}  & \mathbb{E}\!\text{\textit{xt}}^{i+3}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}
(\mathcal{O}_{X_m},\omega_{X_n/A_n}))\\
\cong {} & \mathbb{E}\!\text{\textit{xt}}^{i+3}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}
(\mathcal{O}_{X_m},\mathcal{O}_{X_n}))
\end{align*}
using the Calabi-Yau condition and the hyperext.


However, direct calculation from the resolution \eqref{eq:resolution}
of $\mathcal{O}_{X_m}$ shows that
\[
\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\mathcal{O}_{X_m},\mathcal{O}_{X_n})\cong 
\begin{cases}
\mathcal{O}_{X_m} & q=0;\\
0 & q>0.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus in fact
\begin{align*}
&H^{i}({\bf R}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},
{\bf R}\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\mathcal{O}_{X_m},\omega_{X_n/A_n}[3])))\\
\cong {} & \operatorname{Ext}^{i+3}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_m})\\
\cong {} & \operatorname{Ext}^{i+3}_{\mathcal{O}_{X_m}}(\Omega_{X_m/A_m},\mathcal{O}_{X_m})
\end{align*}
for $i+3\le 2$ by Lemma \ref{2.3}. This shows that the right-hand
vertical side of the diagram of interest agrees with
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:exts}
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_n})
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}}
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{O}_{X_{n-1}}}(\Omega_{X_{n-1}/A_{n-1}},\mathcal{O}_{X_{n-1}})
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\delta}}
\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\Omega_{X},\mathcal{O}_{X}).
\end{equation}
Putting this together with \eqref{eq:dual sequence}, we see we obtain a commutative
diagram with vertical arrows being isomorphisms and rows being exact:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:bob diagram}
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
\operatorname{Hom}_{A_n}(H^2(\Omega_{X_n/A_n}),A_n)\ar[r]\ar[d]&
\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{n-1}}(H^2(\Omega_{X_{n-1}/A_{n-1}}),A_{n-1})
\ar[r]\ar[d]&
\operatorname{Hom}_k(H^1(\Omega_{X/k}),k)\ar[d]\\
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{O}_{X_n}}(\Omega_{X_n/A_n},\mathcal{O}_{X_n})\ar[r]&
\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal{O}_{X_{n-1}}}(\Omega_{X_{n-1}/A_{n-1}},\mathcal{O}_{X_{n-1}})
\ar[r]_>>>>>>{\delta}&
\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\Omega_{X},\mathcal{O}_{X})
}
\end{equation}
This shows that $K$ coincides with ${(\operatorname{im}\delta)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}$.

So the map $H^1(\Omega^1_X)\rightarrow K\rightarrow 0$ is dual to $0\rightarrow
\operatorname{im}\delta\rightarrow T^2$. Thus
${(T^2_{\mathrm{loc}})}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\rightarrow {\operatorname{im}(\delta)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}$ is the surjection
$H^1_Z(\Omega^1_X)\rightarrow K$. This is the desired surjectivity.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{2.6}
We cannot apply Theorem \ref{2.2} immediately to the situation of
Theorem \ref{1.9} without first knowing that $D_{\mathrm{loc}}$ has a hull. By 
\ref{(1.5)}, this is
the case if and only if $T^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X/k)$ is finite dimensional. This is of course
the case if $X$ has isolated singularities, in which case, we can just as well
consider the complex germ $(X,Z)$ instead of the formal scheme $\hat X$.
However, $T^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ need not be finite dimensional
if $X$ has non-isolated
singularities. Nevertheless, even in this case, Theorem \ref{2.2} can be useful. In any
event, Theorem \ref{2.2} tells us that 
$$T^1(X_n/A_n)\rightarrow T^1(X_{n-1}/A_{n-1})\rightarrow T^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$$
is exact. If $T^2_{\mathrm{loc}}=0$, then $D$ is unobstructed by the $T^1$-lifting
criterion. If $T^2_{\mathrm{loc}}\not=0$, then we obtain dimension estimates for
$\operatorname{Def}(X)$ using methods similar to \cite{[19]}. See \cite{[12]} 
for an application in the
non-isolated case. Note in particular that if $X$ has isolated complete
intersection singularities, then $T^2_{\mathrm{loc}}=0$, reproducing the unobstructedness
result of \cite{[28]} in a rather more inefficient way.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
While the proof of Theorem \ref{2.2} only works in dimension three,
the higher-dimensional analogue of the diagram \eqref{eq:bob diagram}
still exists for all $\dim X\ge 3$, with $H^2$ and $H^1$ replaced by $H^{\dim X-1}$ and
$H^{\dim X-2}$ respectively. The proof is the same.

title: Example
body_md:
\label{2.7}
We give here a simple example of a Calabi-Yau with obstructed
deformation theory. Let $Y\subseteq\mathbb{P}^9$ be a cone over a non-singular del Pezzo
surface in $\mathbb{P}^8$ isomorphic to $\mathbb{P}^2$ blown up in one point. By \cite{[2]}, 
a hull of the deformation functor of the singular point of $Y$ is
$\Lambda=k[t]/(t^2)$. In fact, in \cite[(9.2)]{[2]}, Altmann gives explicit equations
for a deformation of the affine cone in ${\bf C}^9$ over the del Pezzo surface
in $\mathbb{P}^8$, and these equations are easily projectivized to yield a non-trivial but
obstructed infinitesimal deformation of $Y$, $\mathcal{Y}/\operatorname{Spec}\Lambda$. 

Let $X$ be a double cover of $Y$ branched over the intersection of $Y$ with a
general quartic hypersurface in $\mathbb{P}^9$. It is easy to see that $K_X=0$, $X$ has two
singular points analytically isomorphic to the singular point of $Y$, and
the deformation $\mathcal{Y}/\operatorname{Spec}\Lambda$ lifts to a deformation $\mathcal{X}/\operatorname{Spec}\Lambda$, 
which is obstructed. In fact, $\operatorname{Def}(X)$ is non-reduced.

See \cite{[11]} for an example in any dimension of obstructed deformations for a
Calabi-Yau with non-isolated singularities. Such an example is much more subtle,
and requires a more global analysis.
head: environment

body_md:
\label{(3.1)} We will first consider, very generally, the situation that $(X,0)$ is the germ
of an isolated rational complex threefold singularity, and that $\pi:(\tilde
X,E)\rightarrow (X,0)$ is a resolution of singularities. We have a natural map of
germs of analytic spaces
$\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X)\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X)$ by \cite[Pro.~11.4]{[23]}, 
(by \cite[Thm.~1.4 (c)]{[48]}
for the map on the level of deformation functors,)
since $H^1(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X})=0$. We denote by $\mathcal{O}_{X,0}$
the local ring of $X$ at the origin with maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$, and we denote by $T^1$
the tangent space of
$\operatorname{Def}(X)$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{3.2} 
The tangent space to $\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X)$ is $H^0(R^1\pi_*
\Theta_{\tilde X})$, of $\operatorname{Def}(X)$ is $T^1=H^2_Z(\Theta_X)$, where $\Theta_X=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_X}
(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_X)$, and there is an exact sequence of $\mathcal{O}_{X,0}$-modules
$$H^0(R^1\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^2_Z(\Theta_X) \rightarrow T'
\rightarrow 0$$ with $T'=\operatorname{ker}(
H^2_E(\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^0(R^2\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X}))$,
$Z=\operatorname{Sing}(X)$ and $E$ the exceptional locus of $\pi$. The map
$H^0(R^1\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^2_Z(\Theta_X)$ is the differential
of the map $\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X)\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $X$ is a germ, $H^1(\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X})=H^2(\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X})=0$.
Thus the tangent space to $\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X)$ is
$H^1(\Theta_{\tilde X})\cong H^0(R^1\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X})$ by the Leray spectral
sequence. Similarly, $H^2(\Theta_{\tilde X})=H^0(R^2\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X})$. Also,
the tangent space to
$\operatorname{Def}(X)$ is 
\[
H^1(X-\{0\},\Theta_X)=H^1(\tilde X-E,\Theta_{\tilde X})=H^2_Z(\Theta_X),
\]
by \cite[Thm.~2]{[42]}. The map 
$H^1(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^1(\tilde
X-E, \Theta_{\tilde X})$
is the differential of $\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X)\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X)$.
Hence the exact sequence
$$H^1(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^1(\tilde X-E,\Theta_{\tilde X})
\rightarrow H^2_E(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^2(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})$$
is identical to
$$H^0(R^1\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^2_Z(\Theta_X)\rightarrow H^2_E(\Theta_{\tilde X})
\rightarrow H^0(R^2\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X})$$
which yields the desired sequence. Elements of
$\mathcal{O}_{X,0}$ pull back to elements of $\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X}$, which then act on $\Theta_{\tilde
X}$, and so
$H^1(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})$ and $H^1 (\tilde X-E,\Theta_{\tilde X})$ are naturally
$\mathcal{O}_{X,0}$-modules.
head: environment

body_md:
\label{(3.3)}
In our situation we will be interested in the case that $(X,0)$ is an isolated
rational Gorenstein point, and that $\tilde X\rightarrow X$ is a crepant
resolution. Recall from \cite{[38]} that there is an invariant $k$ associated with a
rational Gorenstein point as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item[$k=0$] if $(X,0)$ is a cDV point, so is terminal.
\item[$k=1$] if $(X,0)$ is a hypersurface singularity locally of the form $x^2+y^3
+f(y,z,t)=0$ where $f=yf_1(z,t)+f_2(z,t)$ and $f_1$ (respectively $f_2$) is a sum
of monomials $z^at^b$ of degree $a+b\ge 4$ (respectively $\ge 6$). 
\item[$k=2$] if $(X,0)$ is a hypersurface singularity locally of the form
$x^2+f(y,z,t)=0$ where $f$ is a sum of monomials of degree $\ge 4$.
\item[$k\ge 3$] if $mult_0 X=k$ and $emb.dim.(X,0)=k+1$. The exceptional divisor
of the blow-up of $0\in X$ is a del Pezzo surface of degree $k$.
\end{itemize}

So in particular, for $k\le 3$, $(X,0)$ is a hypersurface singularity, and for
$k=4$, $(X,0)$ is a complete intersection (Gorenstein in codimension 2 implies
complete intersection) of two equations whose leading terms are quadratic and
define a del Pezzo surface in $\mathbb{P}^4$.
However
$(X,0)$ is never a complete intersection if
$k>4$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{3.4} 
Let $(\tilde X,E) 
\rightarrow (X,0)$ be a crepant resolution of an
isolated rational Gorenstein threefold singularity $(X,0)$. Then $\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X)$
is non-singular.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Hodge theory of $\tilde X$ is well-behaved above the middle dimension
from \cite{[31]}: in particular the spectral sequence $$H^q(\Omega^p_{\tilde
X})\Rightarrow H^n(\tilde X, \mathbb{C})$$ degenerates at the $E_1$ level for $p+q>3$.
Thus
as in the proof of \cite[5.5]{[4]}, if $\tilde X_n/A_n$ is a
deformation of
$\tilde X$ over $A_n$, then $H^2(\Omega^2_{\tilde X_n/A_n})$ is a locally free
$A_n$-module of rank $\dim H^2(\Omega^2_{\tilde X})$. Then, as a case of
Ran's ``$T^2$-injecting'' criterion \cite{[36]}, we see we have an exact sequence
$$H^1(\Omega^2_{\tilde X_n/A_n})\rightarrow H^1(\Omega^2_{\tilde X_{n-1}/A_{n-1}})
\rightarrow H^2(\Omega^2_{\tilde X})\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\phi}} H^2(\Omega^2_{\tilde X_n/A_n})
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}} H^2(\Omega^2_{\tilde X_{n-1}/A_{n-1}})$$
with $\phi$ injective, so that $T^1(\tilde X_n/A_n)\rightarrow T^1(\tilde X_{n-1}/
A_{n-1})$ is always surjective. Thus, by the $T^1$-lifting criterion,
(Theorem \ref{1.8})  $\operatorname{Def}(\tilde
X)$ is smooth.
head: environment

body_md:
\label{(3.5)}
Suppose furthermore that $X$ is a complete intersection singularity with
a crepant resolution $\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow X$, with
embedding dimension $e$ given by $f_1=\cdots=f_n=0$ with $f_i\in {\bf
C}\{x_1,\ldots,x_e\}$. So $\mathcal{O}_{X,0}=\mathbb{C}\{x_1,\ldots,x_e\}/(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$.
(Of
course, given that
$X$ is a threefold canonical singularity, either $n=1,e=4$ or $n=2,e=5$.) Then
by \cite[pg.~634]{[44]},
$$T^1\cong \mathcal{O}_{X,0}^n/J$$
where $J$ is the submodule of $\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^n$ generated by $(\partial f_1/\partial x_i,
\ldots,\partial f_n/\partial x_i)$, $1\le i\le e$. The obvious $\mathcal{O}_{X,0}$-module
structure on $\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^n/J$ coincides with the $\mathcal{O}_{X,0}$-module structure
on $T^1$ from Lemma \ref{3.2}. If we
choose elements 
\[
(g_{11},\ldots,g_{1n}),\ldots,
(g_{m1},\ldots,g_{mn})\in\mathfrak{m}\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^n
\]
which  along with
$(1,0,\ldots,0),\ldots,(0,\ldots,0,1)$ form a basis for $T^1$ after
reducing modulo $J$, then a miniversal family over the germ $\operatorname{Def}(X)=(T^1,0)$ about
the origin of
$T^1$ is given by
\begin{align*}
f_1+a_1+b_1g_{11}+\cdots+b_mg_{m1} ={} & 0\\
\vdots&\\
f_n+a_n+b_1g_{1n}+\cdots+b_mg_{mn} = {} & 0
\end{align*}
where $a_1,\ldots,a_n,b_1,\ldots,b_m$ are coordinates on $(T^1,0)$ given
by our choice of basis. This
defines a miniversal deformation $F:(\mathcal{X},0)\rightarrow (T^1,0)$ of $(X,0)$. $F$ has a 
discriminant locus $D\subseteq (T^1,0)$, over which the fibres of $F$
are singular. From Lemma \ref{3.2}, we have a quotient $T'$ of $T^1$ which is an
$\mathcal{O}_{X,0}$-module.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{3.6} 
In the situation of \ref{(3.5)}, suppose $(X,0)$ is not an ordinary
double point (analytically isomorphic to $x_1^2+\cdots+x_4^2=0$).
Let ${\bf m}$ be the maximal ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{X,0}$. Then $T'\not=0$ and
if $x\in T'$ is annihilated by
${\bf m}$, then $x\in {\bf m}T'$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We split this into the hypersurface case and the codimension two complete
intersection case, the former being simpler than the latter. First suppose
$(X,0)$ is a hypersurface singularity, so that $T'\cong\mathcal{O}_{X,0}/I$ for some ideal 
$I$ containing the jacobian ideal $J$. If some element of $T'$ not in ${\bf
m}T'$ were annihilated by ${\bf m}$, we would then have a non-zero element of
$T'/{\bf m}T'$ killed by ${\bf m}/{\bf m}^2$ under the surjective multiplication map
$T'/{\bf m}T'
\otimes {\bf m}/{\bf m}^2\rightarrow {\bf m}T'/{\bf m}^2T'$. But $\dim_{\mathbb{C}}
T'/{\bf
m}T'
\le 1$, so this is only possible if ${\bf m}T'=0$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{C}} T'=1$. Thus we
just need to show that $\dim_{\mathbb{C}} T'>1$.

By Proposition \ref{3.4}, 
$\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X)$ is smooth. On the other hand, the fibre of the miniversal
space of $X$ over a general point of $D\subseteq \operatorname{Def}(X)$ has one ODP (\cite[\S5]{[44]}).
I claim that in fact the image of $\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X)$ in $\operatorname{Def}(X)$ cannot contain
any points corresponding to deformations of $X$ to a non-singular germ or a germ
with one ODP, and thus the codimension of the image of $\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X)$ in $\operatorname{Def}(X)$
is at least 2, from which we conclude $\dim T'\ge 2$. To show this claim, if
the invariant $k$ of $(X,0)$ is at least one, then $(\tilde X,0)$ contains some
exceptional divisors, and thus by \cite[Lem.~3.1]{[26]}, any deformation of $(\tilde
X,0)$ does also. Since any deformation of $(\tilde X,0)$ also has trivial canonical
bundle, these divisors blow down to yield a singularity which is not an ODP.
If $k=0$, $\tilde X\rightarrow X$ is a small resolution, and the claim follows from
\cite[Lem.~(1.8)]{[29]}.

In the case that $(X,0)$ is a codimension two complete intersection,
let 
\[
\tilde X
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\pi_1}} X_1\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\pi_2}} X
\]
be a factorization of $\pi$, with $\pi_2$
the blowing up of $X$ at $0$.  By the argument of \cite[(1.5)]{[48]}, we have
$\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_{X_1},\mathcal{O}_{X_1})
\cong \operatorname{Ext}^1(\pi_1^*\Omega^1_{X_1},\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X})$,
$\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_X)
\cong \operatorname{Ext}^1(\pi^*\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X})$, and the natural maps $\pi^*\Omega^1_X
\rightarrow \pi_1^*\Omega^1_{X_1}\rightarrow\Omega^1_{\tilde X}$ induce the maps
on tangent spaces
$$\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde X},\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X})\rightarrow
\operatorname{Ext}^1(\pi_1^*\Omega^1_{X_1},\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X})\rightarrow 
\operatorname{Ext}^1(\pi^*\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X}).$$
Thus if 
$$T''=
\operatorname{coker}(\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_{X_1},\mathcal{O}_{X_1})\rightarrow \operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_X,\mathcal{O}_X)),$$
there is a surjection $T'\rightarrow T''\rightarrow 0$ and it is enough to show
that $T'/\mathfrak{m} T'\cong T''/\mathfrak{m} T''$, $T''\not=0$,
and any element not in ${\bf m}T''$ is not
annihilated by
${\bf m}$. To do this, we consider $X\subseteq Y=({\mathbb{C}}^5,0)$
and $Y_1\rightarrow Y$ the blowing-up
of the origin, $X_1\subseteq Y_1$ the proper transform of $X$ in $Y_1$. We will
first show that every infinitesimal deformation of $X_1$ is a deformation of $X_1$
inside of $Y_1$. We have an exact sequence
$$0\to\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2\to\Omega^1_{Y_1}|_{X_1}\to\Omega^1_{X_1}\to0$$
with $\mathcal{I}$ the ideal sheaf of $X_1\subseteq Y_1$, which yields
$$\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{I}/\mathcal{I}^2,\mathcal{O}_{X_1})\rightarrow\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_{X_1},\mathcal{O}_{X_1})
\rightarrow \operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_{Y_1}|_{X_1},\mathcal{O}_{X_1}).$$
Since $\Omega^1_{Y_1}|_{X_1}$ is locally free, 
$\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_{Y_1}|_{X_1},\mathcal{O}_{X_1})=H^1(\Theta_{Y_1}|_{X_1})$, and we have an exact
sequence
$$H^1(\Theta_{Y_1})\rightarrow H^1(\Theta_{Y_1}|_{X_1})\rightarrow H^2(\Theta_{Y_1}\otimes\mathcal{I}).$$
Let $F$ be the exceptional $\mathbb{P}^4$ of the blowing-up $Y_1\rightarrow Y$. 
Then using 
$$H^1(\Theta_{Y_1})=\lim_{\leftarrow} H^1(\Theta_{Y_1}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{Y_1}/\mathcal{I}_F^n),$$ the exact
sequences
$$0\to\Theta_F\to\Theta_{Y_1}|_F\to\mathcal{O}_F(-1)\to0$$
and
$$0\to\mathcal{O}_F(n-1)=\mathcal{I}_F^{n-1}/\mathcal{I}_F^n\to\mathcal{O}_{Y_1}/\mathcal{I}_F^n\to\mathcal{O}_{Y_1}/\mathcal{I}_F^{n-1}\to0,$$
we see that $H^1(\Theta_{Y_1})=0$. To show that $H^2(\Theta_Y\otimes \mathcal{I})=0$,
we use the Koszul resolution of $\mathcal{I}$
$$0\to\mathcal{L}_1\to\mathcal{L}_2\oplus\mathcal{L}_3\to\mathcal{I}\to0$$
where $\mathcal{L}_1,\mathcal{L}_2$ and $\mathcal{L}_3$ are line bundles, with $\mathcal{L}_1|_F\cong\mathcal{O}_F(-4)$,
$\mathcal{L}_2|_F\cong\mathcal{L}_3|_F\cong\mathcal{O}_F(-2)$. We then see as before that $H^2((\mathcal{L}_2\oplus\mathcal{L}_3)
\otimes\Theta_{Y_1})=0$ and $H^3(\mathcal{L}_1\otimes\Theta_{Y_1})=0$.
Thus $H^2(\Theta_{Y_1}\otimes\mathcal{I})=0$. To conclude, we have shown that
$\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_{Y_1}|_{X_1},\mathcal{O}_{X_1})=0$, and so any infinitesimal deformation of
$X_1$ comes from an  infinitesimal deformation of $X_1$ in $Y_1$. 

Now a choice of $g=(g_1,g_2)\in\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^2$ gives a deformation $\bar X/A_1$ of
$X$ by the equations
\begin{align*}
f_1+tg_1={} & 0\\
f_2+tg_2={} & 0.
\end{align*}
Note that if $\bar X/A_1$ is normally flat along $0\times \operatorname{Spec} A_1$ then
$(g_1,g_2)\in \mathfrak{m}^2\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^2$. Indeed, since $f_1=f_2=0$ defines a rational
Gorenstein singularity, the leading terms of $f_1$ and $f_2$ must be quadratic,
and thus if $(g_1,g_2)\not\in\mathfrak{m}^2\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^2$, the blow-up of $\bar X/A_1$ 
at $0\times\operatorname{Spec} A_1$ would not yield an exceptional divisor flat over $A_1$. 

If we write $T''=\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^2/I$, with $I\supseteq J$, then $(g_1,g_2)\in I$
if $(g_1,g_2)$ yields a deformation $\bar X/A_1$ which lifts to a deformation
$\bar X_1/A_1$ of $X_1$. Since $\bar X_1/A_1$ is equivalent to a deformation
$\bar X_1'/A_1\subseteq Y_1\times\operatorname{Spec} A_1$, we can blow down this deformation
to obtain a deformation $\bar X'/A_1$ equivalent to $\bar X/A_1$, which in
particular is normally flat along $0\times\operatorname{Spec} A_1$. Since two deformations of $X$
given by $(g_1,g_2)$ and $(g_1',g_2')$ are equivalent if and only if
they differ by an element
$(h_1,h_2)\in J$, we must have $(g_1+h_1,g_2+h_2)\in\mathfrak{m}^2\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^2$ for some
$(h_1,h_2)\in J$. 

Now $J\subseteq\mathfrak{m}\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^2$, so if $(g_1,g_2)\not\in\mathfrak{m}\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^2$, we cannot have
$(g_1,g_2)
\in I$. Thus $\dim_{\mathbb{C}}T''/\mathfrak{m} T''=2$, and since $\dim_{\mathbb{C}} T'/\mathfrak{m} T'\le 2$,
we must have the surjection $T'/\mathfrak{m} T'\rightarrow T''/\mathfrak{m} T''$
being an isomorphism, and $T''\not=0$.

If $(g_1,g_2)\not\in\mathfrak{m}\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^2$, but $x_i(g_1,g_2)\in I$ for all $i$, then in
particular for each $i$, there exists $(h_1,h_2)\in J$ such that
$x_i(g_1,g_2)+(h_1,h_2)\in\mathfrak{m}^2\mathcal{O}_{X,0}^2$, from which one easily sees that the
leading (quadratic) terms of $f_1$ and $f_2$ have proportional partial derivatives,
and hence must be proportional themselves, ruling out the possibility of having a del
Pezzo surface as an exceptional divisor. Thus $(g_1,g_2)$ is not annihilated by all
elements of $\mathfrak{m}$ in $T''$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{3.7} 
Let $F':(\mathcal{X}',0)
\rightarrow(\mathcal{S}',0)$ be a flat deformation of
$(X,0)$, with $\mathcal{S}'$
non-singular at $0\in\mathcal{S}'$ and the tangent space at $0\in\mathcal{S}'$ the vector
space
$T$. Assume furthermore that $X$ is not an ordinary double point. Since
$F:(\mathcal{X},0)\rightarrow (T^1,0)$ given in \ref{(3.5)} is a miniversal family for $(X,0)$,
there is a (non-unique) map 
$\mathcal{S}'
\rightarrow (T^1,0)$ inducing a unique differential $T\rightarrow T^1$. Composing this
map with
$T^1\rightarrow T'$, we obtain a map $T\rightarrow T'$. If
$\operatorname{im}(T\rightarrow T')\not\subseteq {\bf m}T'$, then a general fibre of
$\mathcal{X}'\rightarrow\mathcal{S}'$ is non-singular.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Following \cite[pg.~645]{[44]}, let $D\subseteq (T^1,0)$ be the
discriminant locus of $F$, $C\subseteq (\mathcal{X},0)$ the critical locus. From \cite{[44]},
$F|_C:C\rightarrow D$ is the normalization of $D$. If every fibre of $F'$ is
singular, the induced map $\mathcal{S}'\rightarrow (T^1,0)$ factors through $D$.
Since $\mathcal{S}'$ is non-singular, in particular this map
factors through $C\rightarrow D$, and thus
the image of $T$ in $T^1$ is contained in the image in $T^1$ of the tangent space
$T_{\mathcal{X},0}$ of
$(\mathcal{X},0)$ at
$0$ via $F_*$. Using the explicit equations
for $(\mathcal{X},0)$ and basis for $T^1$ given in \ref{(3.5)}, we see that the image of $T_{\mathcal{X},0}$
in
$T^1$ is a vector space
$W\subseteq T^1$ given by
$a_1=\cdots=a_n=0$.
Again from the explicit description of $T^1$ in
\ref{(3.5)}, $W=\mathfrak{m} T^1$, so the image of $W$ in $T'$ is a subspace
$V\subseteq \mathfrak{m} T'$. Thus, we see that if $F'$ only
has singular fibres, the image of $T$ is contained in ${\bf m}T'$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{3.8} 
Let $\tilde X$ be a non-singular Calabi-Yau threefold,
and $\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow X$ be a birational contraction morphism
such that $X$ has isolated, canonical, complete intersection singularities. Then
there is a deformation of $X$ which smooths all singular points of $X$
except possibly the ordinary double points of $X$. In particular, if $X$ has no
ordinary double points, then $X$ is smoothable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $P\in Z=\operatorname{Sing}(X)$ be a singular point of $X$ which is not
an ordinary double point. We will show that there is a deformation of $X$
which smooths $P$. We have a diagram
\begin{equation}
\label{3.9}
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
H^1(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})
\ar[r]& H^1(U,\Theta_{\tilde X}) \ar[r]&H^2_{\pi^{-1}(Z)}(\tilde X,
\Theta_{\tilde X})\ar[r]&H^2(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})\\
& H^1(U,\Theta_{X})\ar[u]^{\cong} \ar[r]&H^2_{Z}(X,
\Theta_{X})\ar[u]&
}
\end{equation}
$\operatorname{Def}(X)$ is smooth by \cite{[28]} or Theorem \ref{2.2}. The second vertical
map arises as in the proof of Lemma \ref{3.2}.
Thus to show that there is a
deformation of
$X$ which smooths
$P\in X$, it is enough to show by Lemma \ref{3.7} that the image of the
composed map 
$$H^1(U,\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^2_{\pi^{-1}(Z)}(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})
\rightarrow H^2_E(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})$$ with $E=\pi^{-1}(P)$ contains
an element not in ${\bf m}_PT'_P
\subseteq T'_P\subseteq H^2_E(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})$. Here ${\bf m}_P$ is the 
maximal ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{X,P}$, and $T'_P$ is the subspace of $H^2_E(\tilde
X,\Theta_{\tilde X})$ given by Lemma \ref{3.2} applied to the germ $(X,P)$. To show this, it is
enough to show that there is an element of $\operatorname{ker}(H^2_E(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\phi}} H^2(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X}))$ not in ${\bf m}_PT'_P$.

To see this, first consider the dual map $$H^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde X})
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{{\phi}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}}} (R^1\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})_P.$$ Since 
$H^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde X})\cong (\operatorname{Pic} \tilde X)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}{\mathbb{C}}$, this
map factors through $\operatorname{Pic}(\tilde X,E)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}{\mathbb{C}}$, where $(\tilde X,E)$
denotes the germ of $\tilde X$ at $E$.
Now let
$E=\bigcup E_i$, with $E_i$ irreducible.

{\it Claim:} The map $\operatorname{Pic}(\tilde X,E)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} {\mathbb{C}}
\rightarrow \bigoplus H^1(\Omega^1_{E_i})$ is injective.

\begin{proof}
Let $(\tilde X',E')\rightarrow (\tilde X,E)$ be a composition
of blow-ups of non-singular subvarieties so that $(\tilde X',E')
\rightarrow (X,P)$ is a resolution with $E'=\bigcup
E'_i$ simple normal crossings. Then we have a diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
0\ar[r]&\operatorname{Pic}(\tilde X',E')\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{C}
\ar[r]&\bigoplus H^1(\Omega^1_{E_i'})\\
&\operatorname{Pic}(\tilde X,E)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{C}\ar[u]
\ar[r]&\bigoplus H^1(\Omega^1_{E_i})\ar[u]\\
&0\ar[u]&
}
\]
The first column is exact since
$\tilde X'\rightarrow \tilde X$ is a series of blow-ups. The map
$\bigoplus H^1(\Omega^1_{E_i})\rightarrow\bigoplus H^1(\Omega^1_{E_i'})$
is defined via the induced maps $E_i'\rightarrow E_j$ for all $i,j$.
Suppose the
first row were exact. Then the claimed map must be injective.

The exactness of the first row follows from an argument of Namikawa in a preprint
version of \cite{[28]}; since this argument did not appear in the final version of the
paper, we sketch it here.

First, by \cite{[38]}, the $E_i'$ are all rational or ruled surfaces, since they are
exceptional divisors in the resolution of a rational Gorenstein point. Let
$\tau_{E'}^p\subseteq \Omega_{E'}^p$ be the torsion subsheaf. Then there is a
spectral sequence
$$E_1^{p,q}=H^q(E',\Omega_{E'}^p/\tau_{E'}^p)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(E',{\mathbb{C}})$$
which degenerates at the $E_1$ term, by \cite[Prop.~1.5]{[7]}. Note that
$H^{p+q}(E',{\mathbb{C}})\cong
H^{p+q}((\tilde X',E'),{\mathbb{C}})$, the cohomology of the germ $(\tilde X',E')$.
Let $$E'_{[p]}=\coprod_{i_0<\cdots<i_p} E_{i_0}'\cap\cdots\cap E_{i_p}'.$$
There is an exact sequence
$$0\rightarrow \Omega_{E'}^p/\tau_{E'}^p\rightarrow
\Omega^p_{E'_{[0]}}\rightarrow\Omega^p_{E'_{[1]}}\rightarrow\cdots$$ for each $p$,
again by \cite[Prop.~1.5]{[7]}.
First consider this sequence for $p=0$. Since $H^2(\mathcal{O}_{E'})=0$, as $(X,P)$ is
a rational singularity, we find $H^1(\mathcal{O}_{E'_{[0]}})\rightarrow H^1(\mathcal{O}_{E'_{[1]}})$
is surjective, and thus $H^0(\Omega^1_{E'_{[0]}})\rightarrow
H^0(\Omega^1_{E'_{[1]}})$ is surjective.

By the same sequence for $p=1$, we find $H^1(\Omega_{E'}^1/\tau_{E'}^1)
\rightarrow H^1(\Omega^1_{E'_{[0]}})$ is injective. With $p=2$, we obtain
$H^0(\Omega_{E'}^2/\tau_{E'}^2)=H^0(\Omega^2_{E'_{[0]}})=0$ since all components
of $E'$ are ruled. Thus our spectral sequence yields $H^2(E',{\mathbb{C}})\cong
H^1(\Omega_{E'}^1/\tau_{E'}^1)$ and so the map $H^2(E',{\mathbb{C}})\rightarrow
H^1(\Omega^1_{E'_{[0]}})$ is injective. Since $\operatorname{Pic}(\tilde X',E')\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}
{\mathbb{C}}\cong H^2((\tilde X',E'),{\mathbb{C}})\cong H^2(E',{\mathbb{C}})$, the result follows.
\end{proof}

Thus the composed map 
$$\operatorname{Pic}(\tilde X,E)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}{\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow
(R^1\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})_P\rightarrow \bigoplus_i  H^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde
X}|_{E_i})$$ must also be injective, as is then the composed map
$$\operatorname{coim}({\phi}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee})\rightarrow (R^1\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})_P
\rightarrow\bigoplus_i H^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde X}|_{E_i}).$$
Dually, we get that the composed map 
$$\bigoplus_i \operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X}}(\mathcal{O}_{E_i},\Theta_{\tilde X})
\rightarrow H^2_E(\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow \operatorname{im}(\phi)$$
is surjective. Now clearly $\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X}}(\mathcal{O}_{E_i},\Theta_{\tilde X})$
is annihilated by the maximal ideal
${\bf m}_P\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{X,P}$ since $\mathcal{O}_{E_i}$ is. Let
$W\subseteq
\bigoplus \operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X}}(\mathcal{O}_{E_i},\Theta_{\tilde X})$ be a subspace mapping 
isomorphically via $\phi$ to $\operatorname{im}(\phi)$. Identifying $W$ with its image
in $H^2_E(\Theta_{\tilde X})$, we must then have $H^2_E(\Theta_{\tilde X})
=W+\operatorname{ker}(\phi)$. $W$ is annihilated by ${\bf m}_P$, and so $W\cap T'_P\subseteq
{\bf m}_PT'_P$ by Lemma \ref{3.6}; since $T_P'\not=0$,  $\operatorname{ker}(\phi)$ contains some elements not in ${\bf
m}_PT'_P$.
