title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(\tilde X',E')\rightarrow (\tilde X,E)$ be a composition
of blow-ups of non-singular subvarieties so that $(\tilde X',E')
\rightarrow (X,P)$ is a resolution with $E'=\bigcup
E'_i$ simple normal crossings. Then we have a diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
0\ar[r]&\operatorname{Pic}(\tilde X',E')\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{C}
\ar[r]&\bigoplus H^1(\Omega^1_{E_i'})\\
&\operatorname{Pic}(\tilde X,E)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{C}\ar[u]
\ar[r]&\bigoplus H^1(\Omega^1_{E_i})\ar[u]\\
&0\ar[u]&
}
\]
The first column is exact since
$\tilde X'\rightarrow \tilde X$ is a series of blow-ups. The map
$\bigoplus H^1(\Omega^1_{E_i})\rightarrow\bigoplus H^1(\Omega^1_{E_i'})$
is defined via the induced maps $E_i'\rightarrow E_j$ for all $i,j$.
Suppose the
first row were exact. Then the claimed map must be injective.

The exactness of the first row follows from an argument of Namikawa in a preprint
version of \cite{[28]}; since this argument did not appear in the final version of the
paper, we sketch it here.

First, by \cite{[38]}, the $E_i'$ are all rational or ruled surfaces, since they are
exceptional divisors in the resolution of a rational Gorenstein point. Let
$\tau_{E'}^p\subseteq \Omega_{E'}^p$ be the torsion subsheaf. Then there is a
spectral sequence
$$E_1^{p,q}=H^q(E',\Omega_{E'}^p/\tau_{E'}^p)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(E',{\mathbb{C}})$$
which degenerates at the $E_1$ term, by \cite[Prop.~1.5]{[7]}. Note that
$H^{p+q}(E',{\mathbb{C}})\cong
H^{p+q}((\tilde X',E'),{\mathbb{C}})$, the cohomology of the germ $(\tilde X',E')$.
Let $$E'_{[p]}=\coprod_{i_0<\cdots<i_p} E_{i_0}'\cap\cdots\cap E_{i_p}'.$$
There is an exact sequence
$$0\rightarrow \Omega_{E'}^p/\tau_{E'}^p\rightarrow
\Omega^p_{E'_{[0]}}\rightarrow\Omega^p_{E'_{[1]}}\rightarrow\cdots$$ for each $p$,
again by \cite[Prop.~1.5]{[7]}.
First consider this sequence for $p=0$. Since $H^2(\mathcal{O}_{E'})=0$, as $(X,P)$ is
a rational singularity, we find $H^1(\mathcal{O}_{E'_{[0]}})\rightarrow H^1(\mathcal{O}_{E'_{[1]}})$
is surjective, and thus $H^0(\Omega^1_{E'_{[0]}})\rightarrow
H^0(\Omega^1_{E'_{[1]}})$ is surjective.

By the same sequence for $p=1$, we find $H^1(\Omega_{E'}^1/\tau_{E'}^1)
\rightarrow H^1(\Omega^1_{E'_{[0]}})$ is injective. With $p=2$, we obtain
$H^0(\Omega_{E'}^2/\tau_{E'}^2)=H^0(\Omega^2_{E'_{[0]}})=0$ since all components
of $E'$ are ruled. Thus our spectral sequence yields $H^2(E',{\mathbb{C}})\cong
H^1(\Omega_{E'}^1/\tau_{E'}^1)$ and so the map $H^2(E',{\mathbb{C}})\rightarrow
H^1(\Omega^1_{E'_{[0]}})$ is injective. Since $\operatorname{Pic}(\tilde X',E')\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}
{\mathbb{C}}\cong H^2((\tilde X',E'),{\mathbb{C}})\cong H^2(E',{\mathbb{C}})$, the result follows.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{3.10} Let $\tilde X$ be a $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial Calabi-Yau threefold with
terminal singularities, and suppose $\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow X$ is a birational
contraction morphism such that $X$ has isolated, canonical, complete intersection
singularities. Then there is a deformation of $X$ to a variety with at worst
ordinary double points.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite{[30]}, there is a small deformation of $\tilde X$, $\tilde\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\Delta$,
such that $\tilde\mathcal{X}_t$, $t\not=0$ is non-singular.
If $H$ is an ample Cartier divisor on $X$,
$\pi^* H$ is a nef and big divisor on $\tilde X$, and by \cite[Prop.~6.1, Thm.~C]{[28]},
this divisor deforms to a relatively nef and big divisor on $\tilde \mathcal{X}$. Thus
the morphism $\pi$ deforms to a morphism
$\pi':\tilde \mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, with $\mathcal{X}$ a deformation of $X$. (It is possible
this may introduce some new ordinary double points on $\mathcal{X}_t$.)
$\mathcal{X}_t$ still has isolated
complete intersection canonical singularities, but has
a crepant resolution $\tilde\mathcal{X}_t\rightarrow\mathcal{X}_t$, so we can apply Theorem \ref{3.8}.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
\label{4.1} Let $S$ be a non-singular del Pezzo surface of degree $\ge 5$,
and consider an elliptic fibration $f:\tilde X\rightarrow S$ defined by the 
Weierstrass equation $y^2=x^3+ax+b$, for general $a\in H^0(\omega_S^{-4})$,
$b\in H^0(\omega_S^{-6})$. $\tilde X$ will be a non-singular Calabi-Yau threefold,
and $f$ has a section $\sigma$, the section at infinity obtained after
compactifying the affine equation given. Identifying $S$ with $\sigma(S)$, it is
possible to find a contraction $\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow X$ contracting $S$. As in
\eqref{3.9}, we
have the exact sequence
$$H^1(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^1(U,\Theta_{\tilde X})
\rightarrow H^2_S(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X}) \rightarrow H^2(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})$$
where $U=\tilde X-S$. Dualizing the last map we obtain the map
$H^1(\tilde X,\Omega^1_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^0(R^1\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})$.
Using $\deg S\ge 5$, a straightforward calculation shows that
\[
H^0(R^1\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})\cong H^1(S,\Omega^1_S),
\]
and $H^1(\tilde X,
\Omega^1_X)\rightarrow H^1(S,\Omega^1_S)$ is the restriction map $\sigma^*$ and is
thus surjective, since $\sigma^*f^*$ is the identity on $H^1(S,\Omega^1_S)$. Thus
$T^1(\tilde X/k)=H^1(\tilde X,\Theta_{\tilde X})
\rightarrow T^1(X/k)=H^1(U,\Theta_{\tilde X})$ is surjective, so
there are no infinitesimal deformations of $X$ which don't 
come from infinitesimal deformations of $\tilde X$. Thus 
$\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X)\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X)$ is surjective.
Since the exceptional locus $S$ deforms in any deformation of $\tilde X$,
$X$ is not smoothable.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
\label{4.2} An isolated non-complete intersection rational Gorenstein
point
$(X,P)$ is {\it good} when
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $X'\rightarrow X$ is the blow-up of $X$ at $P$ with exceptional
divisor $E$, then $E$ is irreducible and $X'$ has only isolated singularities.
\item $\operatorname{Def}(X')$ is non-singular, and the natural map $\operatorname{Def}(X')\rightarrow
\operatorname{Def}(X)$ is an immersion. 
\item There is a smoothing component of $\operatorname{Def}(X)$ containing the image of
$\operatorname{Def}(X')\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X)$. 
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{4.3} 
Let $\tilde X$ be a non-singular Calabi-Yau threefold and
$\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow X$ a birational contraction such that $X$ is 
$\mathbb{Q}$-factorial and for each $P\in \operatorname{Sing}(X)$, $(X,P)$ is good.
Then $X$ is smoothable.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{4.4} 
If $X$ is a compact, $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial algebraic 
variety with rational singularities, $\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow X$
a resolution of singularities with irreducible $E_1,\ldots,E_n\subseteq \tilde X$ the
$\pi$-exceptional divisors, and $H^2(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X})=0$, then
$$\operatorname{im}\left[ H^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde X})\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{p_1}} H^0(R^1\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})
\right]
=\operatorname{im}\left[\bigoplus {\mathbb{C}}E_i\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{p_2}} H^0(R^1\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})
\right]$$
with the map $p_2$ the composition of $\bigoplus{\mathbb{C}}E_i\rightarrow
H^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde X})$ and $p_1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\cite[12.1.6]{[23]} gives a similar statement for rational cohomology,
i.e. $X$ $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial implies that 
$$\operatorname{im}\left[ H^2(\tilde X,\mathbb{Q})\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{p_1}} H^0(X,R^2\pi_*\mathbb{Q})
\right]
=\operatorname{im}\left[\bigoplus \mathbb{Q} E_i\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{p_2}} H^0(X,R^2\pi_*\mathbb{Q})
\right].$$
We can clearly replace $\mathbb{Q}$ by ${\mathbb{C}}$, and since $H^2(\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X})=0$,
$H^2(\tilde X,{\mathbb{C}})=H^1(\tilde X,\Omega^1_{\tilde X})$. Now 
$R^i\pi_*\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X}=0$ for $i>0$ since $X$ has rational
singularities. Thus by the spectral sequence $$R^q\pi_*\Omega^p_{\tilde X}\Rightarrow
R^n\pi_*{\mathbb{C}},$$ there is a natural map
$$H^0(X,R^2\pi_*{\mathbb{C}})\rightarrow H^0(X,R^1\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X}),$$
yielding a commutative diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
H^2(\tilde X,{\mathbb{C}})\ar[r]^{\cong}\ar[d]&H^1(\tilde X,\Omega^1_{\tilde X})
\ar[d]_{p_1}\\
H^0(X,R^2\pi_*{\mathbb{C}})\ar[r]&H^0(X,R^1\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})
}
\]
This gives the desired result.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{4.5} 
Let $\tilde X$ be a non-singular Calabi-Yau threefold, 
$\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow
X$ a birational contraction such that $X$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial with isolated 
singularities. Let $Z=\operatorname{Sing}(X)$, $E=\pi^{-1}(Z)$. Let $T^1$, $T^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ be as in \ref{(2.1)},
the tangent spaces of $\operatorname{Def}(X)$ and $\operatorname{Def}(X,Z)$ respectively, and let
$$T'=\operatorname{ker}(H^2_E(\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^0(R^2\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X}))$$
as in Lemma \ref{3.2}. Then the composed map
$$T^1\rightarrow T^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\rightarrow T'$$
is surjective.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First we claim that
$$\operatorname{ker}(H^2_E(\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^0(R^2\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X}))
=\operatorname{ker}(H^2_E(\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^2(\Theta_{\tilde X})).$$
That the first space contains the second is clear, since the first map factors
through the second. Dualizing this statement, we need to prove that
$$\operatorname{coker}(H^1_E(\Omega^1_{\tilde X})\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{p_1}} H^0(R^1\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X}))
=\operatorname{coker}(H^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde X})\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{p_2}} H^0(R^1\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})).$$
The first surjects on the second, i.e. $\operatorname{im}(p_1)\subseteq
\operatorname{im}(p_2)$. To show equality, we need to show $\operatorname{im}(p_1)\supseteq\operatorname{im}(p_2)$. Let
$\{E_i\}$ be the irreducible components of $E$. We have the diagram
\[
\xymatrix@C=30pt
{
&&0\ar[d]&&\\
&\bigoplus{\mathbb{C}}E_i\ar[r]\ar[d]&\operatorname{Pic}\tilde X\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}{\mathbb{C}}\ar[r]
\ar[d]_{d\log_X}&\operatorname{Pic} U\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}{\mathbb{C}}\ar[r]\ar[d]_{d\log_U}&0\\
0\ar[r]&H^1_E(\Omega^1_{\tilde X})\ar[r]&H^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde X})\ar[r]\ar[d]&
H^1(U,\Omega^1_{\tilde X})&\\
&&0&&
}
\]
Here, $H^0(U,
\Omega^1_{\tilde X})=H^0(U,\Omega^1_X)=0$ by \cite{[43]}. This shows
that $\operatorname{im}(\bigoplus {\mathbb{C}}E_i\rightarrow H^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde X}))
\subseteq \operatorname{im}(H^1_E(\Omega^1_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde X}))$, and
thus by Lemma \ref{4.4} and the hypothesis that $X$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, $\operatorname{im}(p_2)
\subseteq \operatorname{im}(p_1)$. 

Now diagram \eqref{3.9} is still valid in this situation, and we have by definition
$$T'=\operatorname{ker}(H^2_E(\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^0(R^2\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X})),$$
so identifying $T^1$ with $H^1(U,\Theta_X)$, \eqref{3.9} shows that 
$$\operatorname{im}(T^1\rightarrow T')=\operatorname{ker}(H^2_E(\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^2(\Theta_{\tilde X})).$$
The result then follows.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{4.6} 
Let $\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\Delta$ be a one-parameter deformation of
a good singularity $(X,P)$. This induces a map $\Delta\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X)$. Then
either $\operatorname{im}(\Delta\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X))\subseteq \operatorname{im}(\operatorname{Def}(X')\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X))$ or
$\mathcal{X}_t$ has only hypersurface singularities for general $t\in\Delta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that for general $t\in\Delta$, $\mathcal{X}_t$ has worse than hypersurface
singularities. $\mathcal{X}$ must be singular at each point where $\mathcal{X}_t$ has worse than
hypersurface singularities, so we can assume there is a curve $C\subseteq \mathcal{X}$
dominating $\Delta$ along which $\mathcal{X}$ is singular. By making a suitable base change,
we can assume $C$ is the image of a section $\Delta\rightarrow\mathcal{X}$. It is enough to
show that $\mathcal{X}$ is normally flat along $C$; this will permit us to blow up
$\mathcal{X}$ along $C$ to obtain a deformation $\mathcal{X}'\rightarrow \Delta$ of $X'$. To show
that $\mathcal{X}$ is normally flat along $C$, it is enough to show that the multiplicity
of $\mathcal{X}_t$ at $C_t$ is constant for $t\in\Delta$. Indeed, $\mathcal{X}$ is normally flat
along $C$ if the Hilbert-Samuel function of the point $C_t\in\mathcal{X}_t$ is constant for
$t\in\Delta$. For a rational Gorenstein non-cDV point, the exceptional locus
upon blowing-up is a del Pezzo surface, and the Hilbert-Samuel function for a
family of del Pezzo surfaces of the same degree is constant.
 To show that the
multiplicity of
$\mathcal{X}$ along $C$ is constant, it is enough to show the same thing for a general
hyperplane section of $\mathcal{X}$ containing $C$. 

To this end, take a general hyperplane section of $\mathcal{X}$ containing $C$; this yields
a deformation $\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\Delta$ of surface singularities, with $\mathcal{S}_0$ a general
hyperplane section of $\mathcal{X}_0=X$. $\mathcal{S}_0$ is then a Gorenstein elliptic singularity,
and
the blowing up of $\mathcal{S}_0$ at $P$ resolves the singularity, since $(X,P)$ is good.
In particular, if $\tilde\mathcal{S}_0\rightarrow\mathcal{S}_0$ is the blowing up of $\mathcal{S}_0$, then 
the exceptional locus is either a non-singular elliptic curve, a nodal rational
curve, or a cuspidal rational curve. These are the singularities $El(d)$, 
$C(d)$ or $Cu(d)$, where $d$ is the multiplicity of the singularity,
following the notation of \cite[\S5]{[49]}. $\mathcal{S}_t$ must also have elliptic singularities.
If the list of adjacencies given in \cite[\S5]{[49]}, then $\mathcal{S}_0$ can only
be adjacent to an elliptic singularity of the same multiplicity (these are
the adjacencies $Cu(d)\rightarrow C(d)$ and $C(d)\rightarrow El(d)$ in Wahl's notation).
In the case at hand, Wahl's list of adjacencies has been proved to be complete
in \cite{[27]}. Thus the multiplicity of the singularities of $\mathcal{S}_t$ remain constant,
proving the lemma.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will now prove the theorem by constructing a deformation $\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\Delta$
of $X$ such that $\operatorname{im}(\Delta\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X,Z))$ is contained in the smoothing
component given by item (3) of Definition \ref{4.2}, but
$$\operatorname{im}(\Delta\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X,Z))\not\subseteq \operatorname{im}(\operatorname{Def}(X',E')\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X,Z)),$$
where $X'\rightarrow X$ is the blow-up of $X$ at the singular locus $Z$ of $X$,
with exceptional locus $E'$. It will then follow from Lemma \ref{4.6} that
$Y=\mathcal{X}_t$ has only hypersurface singularities for $t\not=0$.
By \cite[12.1.11]{[23]}, $Y$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial. By Corollary \ref{3.10}, 
we can deform $Y$ to something with only ordinary
double points which is still $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, and hence can be smoothed
entirely by \cite{[8]}.

To show this, we will apply Theorems \ref{2.2} and \ref{1.9} to get dimension estimates
of components of $\operatorname{Def}(X)$ versus $Def(X')$. We adopt the following
notation:
\begin{align*}
S:={} & \hbox{the ring which pro-represents the deformation functor of $X$.}\\
\Lambda:={} & \hbox{a hull of the deformation functor of $(X,Z)$.}\\
\Lambda':={} & \hbox{a hull of the deformation functor of $(X',E')$.}\\ 
\tilde \Lambda:= {} & \hbox{a hull of the deformation functor of $(\tilde X,E)$.}\\ 
V_0:= {} & \operatorname{ker}(T^1\rightarrow T^1_{\mathrm{loc}}).\\ 
V_1:={} & \operatorname{coker}(T^1\rightarrow T^1_{\mathrm{loc}}).\\ 
r:={} & \dim V_0.\\ 
s:={} & \dim V_1.\\ 
R:={} & \Lambda[[x_1,\ldots,x_r]].
\end{align*}
By Theorems \ref{2.2} and \ref{1.9},
we have $S\cong R/J$ for some ideal $J\subseteq R$.
Furthermore, there is
an ideal $J'\subseteq J$ with $\operatorname{Supp}(R/J)=\operatorname{Supp}(R/J')$, $\mathfrak{m}_R/(\mathfrak{m}_R^2+J)\cong
\mathfrak{m}_R/(\mathfrak{m}_R^2+J')$ and $J'$ is generated by
$s$ elements.

In addition, we set 
\begin{align*}
p:\operatorname{Spec} R\rightarrow \operatorname{Spec}\Lambda&\quad\hbox{the projection.}\\
\mathscr{C}\subseteq \operatorname{Spec} R&\quad\hbox{the pull-back via $p$ of the smoothing component
given by item (3)}\\
&\quad\hbox{ of Definition \ref{4.2}.}\\
\mathscr{B}\subseteq \operatorname{Spec} R&\quad\hbox{the subscheme defined by $J'$, set-theoretically
equal to $\operatorname{Def}(X)$.}\\
\tilde\mathscr{D}&:=\operatorname{Spec}\tilde\Lambda\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\Lambda} \operatorname{Spec} R.\\ 
f:\tilde\mathscr{D}\rightarrow\operatorname{Spec} R&\quad\hbox{the projection.}\\ 
\mathscr{D}'&:=\operatorname{Spec}\Lambda'\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\Lambda} \operatorname{Spec} R.
\end{align*}
By item
(2) of Definition \ref{4.2}, $\mathscr{D}'$ can be identified with a non-singular subscheme
of $\operatorname{Spec} R$, and $\operatorname{im} f\subseteq\mathscr{D}'$. 

Finally, let $T_{\mathscr{B},0}$, $T_{\mathscr{D}',0}$ and $T_{\tilde\mathscr{D},0}$ be the Zariski
tangent
spaces to $\mathscr{B}$, $\mathscr{D}'$ and $\tilde\mathscr{D}$ at their closed points. $T_{\mathscr{B},0}$ and $T_{\mathscr{D}',0}$
are contained in
$T=T_{\operatorname{Spec} R,0}=T^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\oplus V_0$. 
Then $f_*(
T_{\tilde\mathscr{D},0})\subseteq T_{\mathscr{D}',0}$, and by Lemma \ref{3.2} $f_*(T_{\tilde \mathscr{D},0})$ is the
kernel of the composed map $T\rightarrow T^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\rightarrow T'$.

Note that since $\mathfrak{m}_R/(\mathfrak{m}_R^2+J)\cong
\mathfrak{m}_R/(\mathfrak{m}_R^2+J')$, $T_{\mathscr{B},0}\cong T^1$. Thus
\begin{align*}
\dim (T_{\mathscr{B},0}+T_{\mathscr{D}',0})\ge {} &  \dim(T_{\mathscr{B},0}+f_*(T_{\tilde\mathscr{D},0}))\\
= {} & \dim T_{\mathscr{B},0}
+\dim f_*(T_{\tilde\mathscr{D},0})-\dim T_{\mathscr{B},0}\cap f_*(T_{\tilde\mathscr{D},0})\\
= {} & \dim T'+
\dim
f_*(T_{\tilde\mathscr{D},0}),
\end{align*}
since
$f_*(T_{\tilde\mathscr{D},0})\subseteq T_{\mathscr{D}',0}$ and Lemma \ref{4.5} gives a surjection
$T^1\rightarrow T'$ with kernel $f_*(T_{\tilde\mathscr{D},0})\cap T^1$. 
Also,
$s=\dim T-\dim T_{\mathscr{B},0}=\dim f_*(T_{\tilde\mathscr{D},0})+\dim T'-\dim T_{\mathscr{B},0}$. Then
\begin{align*}
\dim\mathscr{B}\cap\mathscr{D}'\le {} & \dim T_{\mathscr{B},0}\cap T_{\mathscr{D}',0}\\
= {} & \dim T_{\mathscr{B},0}+\dim T_{\mathscr{D}',0}-\dim(T_{\mathscr{B},0}+T_{\mathscr{D}',0})\\
\le {} & \dim T_{\mathscr{B},0}+\dim T_{\mathscr{D}',0}-\dim f_*(T_{\tilde\mathscr{D},0})-\dim T'\\
= {} & \dim T_{\mathscr{D}',0}-s\\
={} & \dim\mathscr{D}'-s.
\end{align*}
On the other hand,
\begin{align*}
\dim\mathscr{B}\cap\mathscr{C}\ge {} & \dim\mathscr{C}-\hbox{\# of equations generating $J'$}\\
={} & \dim \mathscr{C}-s\\
\ge {} & \dim \mathscr{D}'+1-s\quad\quad\hbox{(since $\mathscr{D}'$ is strictly contained in $\mathscr{C}$)}\\
> {} &\dim\mathscr{B}\cap\mathscr{D}'.
\end{align*}
Thus $\mathscr{B}\cap\mathscr{D}'$ is strictly contained in $\mathscr{B}\cap\mathscr{C}$. Thus there is a map $\operatorname{Spec} k[[t]]
\rightarrow \mathscr{B}\cap\mathscr{C}$ whose image is not contained in $\mathscr{B}\cap \mathscr{D}'$. This yields
a small deformation $\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\Delta$ which has the desired properties.

name: Proof of Theorem \ref{4.3}

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{4.7} 
More generally, if every singularity of $X$ is smoothable and,
in the notation of \ref{(2.1)}, $T^1\rightarrow T^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is surjective, then it is clear
that $X$ is smoothable, since then by Theorems \ref{2.2} and \ref{1.9}, any deformation
of $(X,Z)$ is realisable via a deformation of $X$. This will hold, for example, if the map
$H^0(R^1\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X}) \rightarrow H^2_Z(\Theta_X)$ of Lemma \ref{3.2} 
is zero and $X$
is $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{5.1} 
Suppose $\pi:\tilde X\rightarrow X$ is a primitive type I
contraction. Then $X$ is smoothable unless $\pi$ is the contraction of a single
$\mathbb{P}^1$ to an ordinary double point.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $X$ has only ordinary double points, and $C_1,\ldots,C_n$ are the
exceptional curves of $\pi$, then the cohomology classes $[C_1],\ldots,[C_n]\in
H_2(\tilde X,\mathbb{Z})$ coincide, since $\pi$ is primitive, and thus unless $n=1$,
there
is a non-trivial linear dependence relation on $[C_1],\ldots, [C_n]$. Thus by
\cite{[8]}, $X$ is smoothable. If $X$ does not have only ordinary double points,
then let $Z\rightarrow X$ be a (non-projective) small resolution of the ordinary
double points of $X$. Then if $C_1,\ldots,C_n\subseteq Z$ are the exceptional
curves, $[C_1],\ldots,[C_n]=0$ in $H_2(Z,\mathbb{Z})$, and so by \cite[Thm.~2.5]{[29]},
$X$ is smoothable.
head: environment

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{5.3}
While the above theorem was stated for the non-hypersurface
singularity case, in the hypersurface singularity case
we can still rule out the
non-normal case as above, but cones over elliptic curves can, and do, occur.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{5.4} 
Suppose $(X,0)$ is an isolated rational Gorenstein
threefold point with $k=mult_0 X\ge 5$, such that if $\tilde X\rightarrow X$ is the
blowing-up of
$X$ at $0$, then $\tilde X$ is non-singular and the exceptional divisor $E$ is
non-singular. Then $(X,0)$ is analytically isomorphic to a cone over $E$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{I}_E$ be the ideal sheaf of $E$ in $\tilde X$. If $H^1(\Theta_E\otimes
(\mathcal{I}_E/\mathcal{I}_E^2)^n)=H^1((\mathcal{I}_E/\mathcal{I}_E^2)^n)=0$ for all
$n\ge 1$, then \cite[Cor.~to Satz 7]{[9]}, tells us that $(\tilde X,E)$ is
analytically isomorphic to an open neighborhood of $E$ embedded in the normal
bundle of $E$ in $\tilde X$ as the zero section. This will then give the theorem.

$E$ is a del Pezzo surface of degree between 5 and 9, and
$\mathcal{I}_E/\mathcal{I}_E^2=\omega^{-1}_E$. For a del Pezzo surface, $H^1(\omega_E^{-n})=0$ for
all $n\ge 1$. If we show that $H^1(\Theta_E)=0$, then if $H$ is a hyperplane section of
$E$, the exact sequence
$$0\to\Theta_E\otimes\omega_E^{-n+1}\to\Theta_E\otimes\omega_E^{-n}\to(\Theta_E\otimes\omega_E^{-n})|_H\to0$$ shows us that $H^1(\Theta_E\otimes\omega^{-n}_E)=0$
for all $n\ge 1$. Now $E$ is $\mathbb{P}^2$, $\mathbb{P}^1\times\mathbb{P}^1$, or $\mathbb{P}^2$ blown up in
$9-k$ points. In the first two cases, $H^1(\Theta_E)=0$ is immediate. In the other
cases, $H^1(\Theta_E)$ is the tangent space to $\operatorname{Def}(E)$, and the moduli space of
non-singular del Pezzo surfaces of degree $\ge 5$ consists of a single point
(reduced since $H^2(\Theta_E)\cong {H^0(\Omega^1_E\otimes\omega_E)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}=0$) by \cite[VII, 2]{[5]}.
Thus $H^1(\Theta_E)=0$.
head: environment

body_md:
\label{(5.5)}
We review here the deformation theory of the singularity $(X,0)$ which is
the
cone over a non-singular del Pezzo surface $E$ of degree $k$, $5\le k\le 9$. The
cases
$6\le k\le 9$ follow from \cite{[2]}.
\begin{itemize}
\item[$k=9$:] $(X,0)$ is rigid. (This also follows from \cite{[42]}.)
\item[$k=8$:] There are two cases. If $E\cong\mathbb{P}^1\times\mathbb{P}^1$, then $(X,0)$ can be
smoothed by taking a hyperplane section of a cone over $\mathbb{P}^3$ embedded via the
2-uple embedding. If $E\cong F_1$, there is no smoothing. In both cases, $\dim_k
T^1=1$. 
\item[$k=7$:] $(X,0)$ can be smoothed by taking a hyperplane section of a cone over
$\mathbb{P}^3$ blown up at a point, embedded in $\mathbb{P}^8$ by projecting $\mathbb{P}^3$ embedded
in $\mathbb{P}^9$ via the 2-uple embedding from a point on the $\mathbb{P}^3$. Here $\dim_k
T^1=2$.
\item[$k=6$:] There are two distinct smoothings, one coming from taking a hyperplane
section of a cone over $\mathbb{P}^1\times\mathbb{P}^1\times\mathbb{P}^1\subseteq \mathbb{P}^7,$ the other
from taking two hyperplane sections of a cone over $\mathbb{P}^2\times\mathbb{P}^2\subseteq\mathbb{P}^8$.
Here $\dim_k T^1=3$.
\item[$k=5$:] Any codimension 3 Gorenstein subscheme of the spectrum of a regular
local ring is a Pfaffian subscheme \cite{[3]}, and any Pfaffian subscheme is
smoothable by \cite{[22]}. Here
$\dim_k T^1=4$.
\end{itemize}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{5.6} 
Let $E$ be a del Pezzo surface which is either rational
and normal of any degree or else
is non-normal of degree 7 of type (ii) (a) or (b) as given in the proof of Theorem
\ref{5.2}.
Then
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $H^2(\Theta_E\otimes \omega_E^{-n})=0$ for all $n\ge 0$.
\item[(ii)] $H^2(\Omega^1_E\otimes \omega_E^{-n})=0$ for all $n\ge 0$.
\item[(iii)] $E$ is smoothable.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) By Serre duality, ${H^2(\Theta_E\otimes\omega_E^{-n})}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\cong H^0(
{{\Omega^1_E}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\otimes\omega_E^{n+1})$. If $E$ is a normal
del Pezzo surface and thus has only quotient singularities, then
$H^0({{\Omega^1_E}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee})=0$ by Hodge theory. Since $\omega_E^{-1}$ is
effective, $H^0({{\Omega^1_E}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\otimes \omega_E^{n+1})=0$ for all 
$n\ge 0$ also.

If $E$ is non-normal, let $n:\tilde E\rightarrow E$ be the normalization, so 
that $\tilde E$ is a scroll. Then the map $n^*\Omega^1_E\rightarrow
\Omega^1_{\tilde E}$ yields a map ${{\Omega^1_E}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\rightarrow
{{(n_*\Omega^1_{\tilde E})}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}\cong n_*\Omega^1_{\tilde E}$,
as is seen by applying duality for a finite morphism twice 
(\cite[III Ex. 6.10 b)]{[16]}
and  \cite{[39]}).
Since
${{\Omega^1_E}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}$ is torsion-free, this map is injective, so
$H^0({{\Omega^1_E}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee})\subseteq H^0(\Omega^1_{\tilde E})=0$. Thus the
result still follows in this case.

(ii) If $E$ is normal, then again
$H^2(\Omega^1_E)\cong H^2({{\Omega^1_E}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee})=0$ by Hodge theory, and so (ii)
follows. Now suppose $E$ is not normal, with $n:\tilde E\rightarrow E$ the
normalization. We need to consider type (ii) (a) and (b) separately. If $E$ is of
type (a), $n$ maps the section $C_0$ two-to-one to the singular curve $l$. Let
$\iota:C_0\rightarrow C_0$ be the induced involution on $C_0$. $\iota$ 
induces an involution $\iota^*:n_*\Omega^1_{C_0}\rightarrow n_*\Omega^1_{C_0}$.
Let $\mathcal{F}\subseteq n_*\Omega^1_{C_0}$ be the sheaf of anti-invariants of this
involution. $\mathcal{F}$ is the image of the map
$\delta':n_*\Omega^1_{C_0}\rightarrow n_*\Omega^1_{C_0}$ given by $\delta'(\alpha)=
\alpha-\iota^*(\alpha)$. Since $n_*\Omega^1_{C_0}=n_*\mathcal{O}_{C_0}(-2)=\mathcal{O}_l(-2)\oplus
\mathcal{O}_l(-1)$, in fact $\mathcal{F}\cong\mathcal{O}_l(-1)$. Let $\tau^1_E\subseteq\Omega^1_E$ be the
torsion subsheaf of $\Omega^1_E$. We then have a complex
\begin{equation}
\label{(5.7)}
0\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}} \tau^1_E \smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}}\Omega^1_E\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}} n_*\Omega^1_{\tilde E}
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{\delta}} \mathcal{F}\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}} 0
\end{equation}
where $\delta$ is the (surjective) composition of the surjective restriction map
$n_*\Omega^1_{\tilde E}\rightarrow n_*\Omega^1_{C_0}$ and $\delta'$. This sequence
is exact at $\Omega^1_E$ since $n_*\Omega^1_{\tilde E}$ is torsion-free. It is
exact at $n_*\Omega^1_{\tilde E}$ where $E$ has normal crossings by \cite[(1.5)]{[7]},
and thus this complex splits into exact sequences
$$0\toK\ton_*\Omega^1_{\tilde E}\to\mathcal{F}\to0$$
and 
$$0\to\Omega^1_E/\tau^1_E\toK\to\tau'\to0$$
with $\tau'$ supported on points, from which we conclude that $H^2(\Omega^1_E)=0$
as desired, and (ii) follows in this case. 

If $E$ is of case (ii) (b), then we can follow a similar procedure. The
normalization map $n$ maps $C_0$ and $f$ to the singular line $l$. Let $\iota:
C_0\coprod f\rightarrow C_0\coprod f$ be the induced involution interchanging
these two lines. This induces $\iota^*: n_*\Omega^1_{C_0\coprod f}
\rightarrow n_*\Omega^1_{C_0\coprod f}$; let $\mathcal{F}\cong \Omega^1_l$ be the
anti-invariant part. Again, $\mathcal{F}$ is the image of $\delta':n_*\Omega^1_{C_0\coprod f}
\rightarrow n_*\Omega^1_{C_0\coprod f}$ given by
$\delta'(\alpha)=\alpha-\iota^*(\alpha)$. We still have the complex 
\eqref{(5.7)}, 
and we finish the argument as before, noting now that the map $H^1(\Omega^1_{\tilde
E})\rightarrow H^1(\mathcal{F})$ is surjective.


(iii) A nodal del Pezzo surface is easily seen to be smoothable: the local-global $\operatorname{Ext}$
sequence yields
$$\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_E,\mathcal{O}_E)\rightarrow H^0(\underline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1(\Omega^1_E,\mathcal{O}_E)) \rightarrow
H^2(\Theta_E)=0,$$ 
and since $\operatorname{Def}(E)$ is smooth, any small deformation of a neighborhood of the
rational double points of $E$ is realised by a global deformation of $E$.

If $E$ is not normal, then $E$ is degree 7 of type (ii) (a) or (b). First suppose
$E\subseteq\mathbb{P}^7$ is of type (ii) (a). Then there is a map $p:E\rightarrow l$
taking a point $x\in E$ to the point of $l\subseteq E$ which is contained in the
same ruling of $E$ as $x$. Each fibre is a singular conic: a union of two $\mathbb{P}^1$'s
or in two cases a doubled line. Each conic spans a plane, and thus $E$ is contained
in a three dimensional scroll. Abstractly, this scroll can be described as the image
of the $\mathbb{P}^2$-bundle $\mathbb{P}(p_*\mathcal{O}_E(1))$ in $\mathbb{P}^7$. Note that $p_*\mathcal{O}_E(1)$ is
generated by global sections since $\mathcal{O}_E(1)$ is. Since
$h^0(p_*\mathcal{O}_E(1))=h^0(\mathcal{O}_E(1))=8$, $p_*\mathcal{O}_E(1)$ must be a rank $3$ vector bundle on
$l$ isomorphic to
$\mathcal{E}_{(a,b,c)}=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(a)\oplus\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(b)\oplus\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1}(c)$ with
$a,b,c\ge 0$ and $a+b+c+3=8$.
If $t=c_1(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{(a,b,c)})}(1))$ and $f$ is the class of a fibre
of $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{(a,b,c)})$, then $\operatorname{Pic}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{(a,b,c)})=\mathbb{Z} t\oplus\mathbb{Z} f$. In order
for $E\subseteq \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{(a,b,c)})$ to be a conic bundle of degree $7$, it must
have class $2t-3f$. The linear system $|t|$ induces the map of $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{(a,b,c)})$
into $\mathbb{P}^7$, and if $|t|$ were not ample (i.e. one of $a$, $b$, or $c$ were zero),
it is easy to see that this would imply two different fibres of $p$ were not
disjoint.
Thus $(a,b,c)=(1,2,2)$ or $(1,1,3)$. In the latter case, the linear system
$|2t-3f|$ has a fixed component given by $t-3f$, and so
$E\subseteq\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{(1,2,2)})$.

Now a non-singular del Pezzo surface $E'$ of degree 7 also has a conic bundle
structure, so an identical argument also shows that $E'\subseteq\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{(1,2,2)})$
and is in the same linear system $|2t-3f|$. Thus $E$ is smoothable.

If $E$ is of type (ii) (b), it is easy to see that it is a degenerate case of (ii)
(a),   and so this case is also  smoothable. One can consult \cite{[51]} for an
explicit description of this degeneration.

title: Proof
body_md:
We want to apply Theorem \ref{4.3}, so we need to verify the hypotheses of the
theorem. First, since $\pi$ corresponds to the contraction of an extremal ray
corresponding to $K_{\tilde X}+E$, $X$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial by \cite[Prop.~5.1.6]{[20]}.

From now on we will assume that $k\ge 5$. If $k\le 4$, then $X$ has only complete
intersection singularities and we can apply Theorem \ref{3.8}. We have to show that the
singularity of $X$ is good.

Let $P\in X$ be the singular point, with $(\tilde X,E)\rightarrow (X,P)$ the
resolution of the germ $(X,P)$. We first consider deformations of the 
inclusion map $i:E\rightarrow (\tilde X,E)$ of $E$ into
the germ $(\tilde X,E)$. If we denote by $T^1_i$ the tangent
space to the deformation space of the triple $((\tilde X,E), E, i)$, there is an
exact sequence by \cite{[32]}
\begin{align*}
&\operatorname{Hom}(\Omega^1_E,\mathcal{O}_E)\oplus H^0(\Theta_{\tilde X})\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}}
H^0(\Theta_{\tilde X}|_E)\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}}T^1_i\\
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{(d_1,d_2)}}&
\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_E,\mathcal{O}_E)\oplus H^1(\Theta_{\tilde X})
\smash{
  \mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits^{}} H^1(\Theta_{\tilde X}|_E).
\end{align*}
Here, by $H^i(\Theta_{\tilde X})$, we mean cohomology on the germ $(\tilde X,E)$.
Note that $\tilde X$ is non-singular but $E$ may not be. The composed maps 
$d_1:T^1_i\rightarrow\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_E,\mathcal{O}_E)$ and $d_2:T^1_i\rightarrow
H^1(\Theta_{\tilde X})$ are the differentials of the maps 
$\operatorname{Def}((\tilde X,E),E,i)\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(E)$ and $\operatorname{Def}((\tilde X,E),E,i)\rightarrow
\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X,E)$ respectively. 

{\it Claim 1:} $d_1$ and $d_2$ are surjective.

\begin{proof}
Note that $d_2$ is surjective if the map $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_E,\mathcal{O}_E)\rightarrow
H^1(\Theta_{\tilde X}|_E)$ is surjective, which is the case since
$H^1({(\mathcal{I}_E/\mathcal{I}_E^2)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee})= H^1(\omega_E)=0$. (In fact, since
$H^0({(\mathcal{I}_E/\mathcal{I}_E^2)}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee})=0$ also, this map is an isomorphism.) Similarly,
$d_1$ is surjective if
$H^1(\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^1(\Theta_{\tilde X}|_E)$ is surjective, which is true if
\[
H^2(\Theta_{\tilde X}(-E))=\lim_{\leftarrow} H^2(\Theta_{\tilde X}(-E)\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\tilde
X}/\mathcal{I}_E^n)=0.
\]
From
$$0\to\Theta_E(-E)\to\Theta_{\tilde X}(-E)|_E\to\mathcal{O}_E\to0$$
we see that $H^2(\Theta_{\tilde X}(-E)|_E)=0$ if
$H^2(\Theta_E(-E))=H^2(\Theta_E\otimes\omega_E^{-1})=0$. This is the case by Lemma \ref{5.6} (i).
Tensoring the exact sequence
$$0\to\mathcal{I}_E^n/\mathcal{I}_E^{n+1}=\omega_E^{-n}\to\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X}/\mathcal{I}_E^{n+1}\to\mathcal{O}_{\tilde X}
/\mathcal{I}_E^n\to0$$ 
with $\Theta_{\tilde X}(-E)$ shows that $H^2(\Theta_{\tilde X}(-E)\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\tilde
X}/\mathcal{I}_E^n)=0$ for all $n$, so $d_1$ is surjective. 
\end{proof}

{\it Claim 2:} $\operatorname{Def}((\tilde X,E), E, i)$ is unobstructed.

\begin{proof}
As noted in the proof of Claim 1, the map $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Omega^1_E,\mathcal{O}_E)
\rightarrow H^1(\Theta_{\tilde X}|_E)$ is an isomorphism. Also the map
$\operatorname{Hom}(\Omega^1_E,\mathcal{O}_E)\rightarrow H^0(\Theta_{\tilde X}|_E)$ is a surjection. This
shows that $T^1_i\cong H^1(\Theta_{\tilde X})$, and it then follows from Proposition
\ref{3.4} as in the proof of \cite[Thm.~2.1]{[35]}, that $\operatorname{Def}((\tilde X,E), E, i)$ is
unobstructed. 
\end{proof}

Thus, since $d_2$ is surjective by Claim 1, any
deformation of $(\tilde X,E)$ is of the form $(\tilde X',E')$ with $E'$
a deformation of $E$. Since $d_1$ is surjective, for any small deformation of $E$
to $E'$, there is a deformation $(\tilde X',E')$ of $(\tilde X,E)$. Thus in
particular, if $E$ is smoothable, the general deformation of $(\tilde X,E)$
to $(\tilde X',E')$ yields $E'$ smooth. By Lemma \ref{5.6} (iii),
any of the possible del
Pezzo surfaces under consideration are smoothable.

To summarize, $(\tilde X,E)$ can be deformed to $(\tilde X',E')$ with $E'$
non-singular. So $(X,P)$ can be deformed to $(X',P')$ with $(\tilde
X',E')\rightarrow
(X',P')$ the blow-up, and by Theorem \ref{5.4}, $(X',P')$ is analytically isomorphic to
a cone over a del Pezzo surface. By \ref{(5.5)}, $(X',P')$ is smoothable unless
$E'\cong\mathbb{P}^2$ or $F_1$. In this latter case, as it is easy to see that the only
normal del Pezzo surfaces of degree $8$ or $9$ are $\mathbb{P}^2$, $F_1$,
$\mathbb{P}^1\times\mathbb{P}^1$ or a quadric cone appropriately embedded, we must also have
$E\cong\mathbb{P}^2$ or $F_1$.

If $E$ is not $\mathbb{P}^2$ or $F_1$, then $(X',P')$ is smoothable. Thus the general
point in the image of $\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X,E)\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X,P)$ is smoothable, so this
image is contained in a smoothing component. The only remaining thing to check is
that $\operatorname{Def}(\tilde X,E)\rightarrow \operatorname{Def}(X,P)$ is an immersion. Thus we need to show
that the differential of this map is injective. This differential
is given by Lemma
\ref{3.2} to be the map
$H^0(R^1\pi_*\Theta_{\tilde X})\rightarrow H^2_Z(\Theta_X)$, and the kernel of this map is
$H^1_E(\Theta_{\tilde X})\cong
{H^0(R^2\pi_*\Omega^1_{\tilde X})}^{\scriptscriptstyle \vee}$, which is
easily seen to be zero using similar methods as above via Lemma \ref{5.6} (ii).
